AC5 pinned in widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-two-tabs.test.ts (2026-09-25, two stores over one jsdom localStorage), the US-10 AC5 block (13: a tab with nothing unsaved writes nothing; an unsaved edit writes the merge and moves the version on; two tabs in one slot keep both rows, one active; an erase in the other tab stands, with or without an unsaved edit; a newer app's record is never written over, and the refusal is reported; a save that failed on a full disk is written by the close once there is room; a hide that merges the other tab's erase takes it in (drafts cleared, the page told, a later edit kept); after it, an erase here removes what the other tab saved since; after a hide the tab shows what the other tab saved at once, and its next save runs without a conflict and takes in what came after; a second hide with nothing new writes nothing; a device that refuses every write reports each kind of refusal once per page load; a conflict with another tab is retried on every hide, though an earlier one was too), the adapter's own test (writeSync refuses a version another tab moved), plus roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts (a cloud tab with nothing unsaved reads and writes nothing on hide; a hide retries a cloud save that failed). AC6 pinned in merge.test.ts (14: the height-and-birth-year race both ways round, two devices' screening answers, the same field on both, two pre-stamp files merging field by field (2026-09-26; before, the whole newer object), Codex's three-copy order case and two unstamped copies tied on both clocks with a stamped third (2026-09-26, both failed before), a pre-stamp copy against a stamped one, a stamped copy an older app wrote over, three devices converging in any order with a merge of the merge changing nothing, stampFields stamping only what it writes and re-stamping an older app's write, a field one copy never had, and the erase gate with and without keepNewerThan), merge-clocks.test.ts (the stamp invariant, and since 2026-09-26 the join laws: 3,000 seeded triples of stamped, legacy, stale, hand-edited and empty copies, with ties and nulls, commutative, associative in three orders, idempotent and absorbing on values and stamps; it failed before on the invariant and on idempotence), migrate.test.ts (2: field stamps sanitised, none added; a missing or mistyped updatedAt read as ""), merge.test.ts again (2026-09-26: a later null beats an older value, a later value beats an older null, a cleared field survives a re-merge), roadmap-file.schema.test.ts (2026-09-26, US-29: a cleared profile field and a blank numeric screening answer, through stampFields, merge and migrate, validate, which failed before; every field of both objects takes null and refuses an object; no clock takes null), mcp-tools.test.ts (2: update_profile stamps only the fields it changes, read_record leaves the stamps out), roadmap-store.test.ts (3: two stores over one cloud, a pre-stamp record; a height against a birth year and a units switch, a height against the email flag, two screening answers) and roadmap-file.schema.test.ts (a stamped record validates; a stamp without its time does not). Hydration gate (AC1) lives in HealthTool UI — still untested, accepted. Writing these tests immediately caught a real defect — see US-11. ✅ Real WebKit, 2026-09-25 (iPhone 13 emulation, the live page with the local build of 650c39f swapped in, every POST and tracker blocked): a stale tab's reload writes nothing and the other tab's rows survive; a reload with an unsaved edit makes one merged write holding both tabs' rows; a stale tab that hides after the other tab's erase writes the erased record, takes the erase in and drops its draft. The pre-fix build fails all three. Live on health-roadmap-edu-90, where tools/webkit-verify.mjs passed on desktop and iPhone. ✅ Real WebKit, 2026-09-25 (same harness): tab B set a height of 181, stale tab A set a birth year of 1980, and the stored profile kept both, with field stamps; the pre-change build kept A's old height. Live on health-roadmap-edu-91.

US-11 · Deleting my data

As a user, I can erase everything from the tool on every device (eraseEpoch bump + empty flush); there is no server copy to chase. Since US-09 AC23 the erase removes every row it can see in this browser and the connected cloud file; a value another device has not yet saved, or saves while the erase runs, is kept and arrives later; for a guest erase, "With no cloud connected, the values in this browser are erased. If you later connect a cloud, the same values are erased there too and its profile and screening answers are reset; values this browser never held stay." The confirm, the alert and the privacy addendum say so (HealthTool.erase-copy.test.ts).

  • AC1 (2026-09-10): an erase clears the health data that sits OUTSIDE the record file, in every mode. The uploaded document blobs (health_roadmap_doc_v2:*) and both matrices' typed-but-unsaved drafts (health_roadmap_bt_timeline_draft, and health_roadmap_vitals_draft since 2026-09-24) go by name, and so, since 2026-10-13, do the Lp(a) check's kept answers (health_roadmap_lpa_check_kept, US-05 AC3), which name rows of the record. Before this, a localStorage-only user kept every document blob: the residue wipe ran only with a cloud connected, because it goes through LocalStorageAdapter.disconnect(), which in local mode would delete the erased file the erase had just written; and the draft survived an erase on every backend. The clear is a NAMED list, never a prefix wipe. health_roadmap_* also holds the cloud tokens, the remembered backend, the device id and the consent keys (hr_reminders_autoenrol_blocked, hr_ab, hr_vid), and taking those would log the user out and reset decisions they had already made. hr_anthropic_key stays as well: it is a credential the user typed, not health data. The notice now says what an erase cannot reach: the original documents already in the user's cloud folder, which no adapter deletes, and the provider's version history, GitHub keeping every past version. Tests: widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts, "RoadmapStore.deleteUserData clears off-file health data (US-11 AC1)" (3: local mode, cloud mode, and the keep-list of tokens, consent flags and the typed API key).
  • AC2 (2026-09-10): an erase reaches chat-history.json. The record erase never touched it, so every conversation the user had ever held stayed in their cloud folder. It cannot be emptied by writing an empty file: the chat merge unions conversations by id, so any other device's copy would put them all back. So the erase TOMBSTONES every conversation instead (deleted: true, no messages, blank title, bumped updatedAt) and a tombstone is monotonic. The title is blanked because it is the user's own first sentence; the merge now drops a tombstone's title the way it already dropped its messages, so a same-millisecond tie cannot bring it back. It runs through the getChatHistory() singleton, so an open chat panel's own instance is the one erased, and BEFORE the record erase. Best-effort like the reminder hook: a failure goes to Sentry and never blocks the erase. Tests: widget-src/src/storage/chat-history-store.test.ts (4: tombstones all, merge with a pre-erase copy keeps the tombstones and the blank titles, a later recordExchange is refused, an empty history writes nothing), packages/health-core/src/chat-history.test.ts ("deleted is a monotonic tombstone and clears messages and the title"), widget-src/src/lib/local-first-data.test.ts (2: the erase tombstones history, and the record is erased even when the chat write fails).
  • AC2b (2026-10-21, D4 decision D2): a conversation deleted, or every conversation erased, while a chat save is still in the air stays deleted on screen. The cloud save used to put its result in place of the working copy, so a save that started before the delete and answered after it brought the conversation back until a reload (the cloud file kept the tombstone). The save's result is now merged into the working copy (health-core ChatSession). The erase order moves into the record session with it (RecordSession.deleteAllData, O6): read the record, then the reminders teardown, then the chat tombstones, then the record erase, each step best-effort and reported. Tests: chat-history-in-flight.test.ts (failed first: a delete, and an erase, during an in-flight save), chat-session.test.ts, record-session.session.test.ts (the order, a failed step reported and the erase still made, neither step on a refused erase).
  • AC3 (2026-09-10): a localStorage-only user's health_roadmap_file_v2:chat-history.json is removed by the erase. Only LocalStorageAdapter.disconnect() clears that prefix, and local mode skips disconnect (it would delete the erased record file itself), so the keys survived. The erase now sweeps the named-file prefix in local mode, which leaves the record file alone because its keys carry no colon. Order matters: the tombstone goes through the singleton FIRST, then the keys go — the other way round, a live store instance would conflict, re-read null, merge and resurrect. Test: widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts, "removes the named record files (chat history) but keeps the erased record file".
  • AC3b: Completed local named-file cleanup invalidates stale local chat stores through a separate content-free generation marker that survives a later disconnect. A stale store's next ordinary read or write cannot restore the erased conversation; fresh chat remains possible. Chat does not parse unrelated roadmap JSON. The marker holds no conversation content, IDs, health values or timestamps and is not sent to cloud storage. A failed marker write reports incomplete cleanup as a warning, not a refusal: the record IS erased, so an erase answers {success:true, warning:"Could not complete on-device history cleanup."}, and the page still clears the chat's copy of the record (health_roadmap_data), mutes the embed, resets the form and shows the warning after the erase notice (AC8; Codex R2, adversary R1). Any failure after the erase's flush landed is a warning the same way; a refused erase (ERASE_UNREACHABLE, a failed flush) still answers {success:false} and rotates no marker. The chat and document keys are still gone (documents are removed before the marker is written). An answer that arrives after a local erase is not saved under a conversation the erase removed: each local chat store remembers, in memory only, the ids it held when it saw the marker change, and refuses them; a new conversation still saves (US-11 AC2, Codex R1). Known residual: the first answer of a conversation that held no saved exchange before the erase is saved, as on a cloud. Log-off is not stopped by it (US-09 AC2c). This does not make simultaneous localStorage operations transactional. Tests: widget-src/src/storage/chat-history-local-erase.test.ts (failed marker write in local and cloud mode; an answer landing after the erase in the erasing and a stale tab; a refused erase leaves the marker unchanged; independent stores over shared synthetic localStorage, not real multi-process browser proof), widget-src/src/components/HealthTool.chat-profile.test.tsx (the deletion flow with the mirror seeded and the marker write failing).
  • AC4 (2026-09-10): an erase turns reminders OFF for anyone who had them on. Erasing an active opt-in left no reminderOptIn at all, which reads as "never decided", so the next storefront load auto-enrolled the user again through the address lane — refilling the server row the pre-erase hook had just torn down, with no token left in the widget to cancel it. The erased file now carries reminderOptIn: { status: 'cancelled' } whenever there WAS an opt-in, active or cancelled, and still carries no token or address. The manual toggle re-enrols, because that is the user asking. What that re-enrolment then does, on the address lane (Dropbox, GitHub, typed): it hits the existing US-17 AC8 path — the server refills the surviving row's schedule and returns no token, so the widget control keeps reading "Turn on" while the reminders send. Google Drive is unaffected: a Google-verified cancel deletes the row outright, so a Drive re-enrolment is a genuinely new one and gets its token. This is pre-existing behaviour for any existing row, not something the erase introduced; it is stated here because after an erase it becomes the normal path rather than the edge case. Tests: widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts (2: an enrolled user comes out cancelled with no identity; a user who never decided still comes out with no record).
  • AC5 (2026-09-10): the caveats are in the CONFIRM, not the alert afterwards. "This will permanently delete all your health data" was a promise the app cannot keep, and the things it cannot reach arrived after the click, too late to be a decision. The confirm now says what is erased (the health record and the chat history), then names the copies that stay: uploaded documents already in the cloud folder, connector import candidates (imports/pending-*.json) until the next import, the provider's version history and GitHub's past commits, and the command-line tool's backups beside the file, which stay only until that tool next writes the file (an erase write keeps no backup, and every later write prunes the copies that predate the erase epoch). The post-erase alert says the same things, shorter, and has a second form for the erase whose chat-history write failed: deleteUserData() swallows that failure so an unreachable cloud cannot trap the user's data on their device, and now RETURNS chatErased, so the alert says the chat history could not be reached and is erased on the next chat (true: the tombstones sit in the getChatHistory() singleton and the next recordExchange merges them through sync.save) instead of claiming a deletion that did not happen. Tests: widget-src/src/components/HealthTool.erase-copy.test.ts (8, against the ERASE_CONFIRM/ERASE_DONE/ERASE_DONE_CHAT_PENDING constants that drive the dialogs — including that the confirm never claims the row stops reminders restarting), widget-src/src/lib/local-first-data.test.ts ("erases the record even when the chat-history write fails, and says so" asserts chatErased: false).
  • AC6 (2026-09-24): an erase made on another device clears this device's drafts when this device takes it in, by a re-read or by a save: both drafts go by name, as in AC1, and since 2026-10-13 the Lp(a) check's kept answers too (Codex R2, adversary R7). Another tab of the same browser counts: its erase comes in by the re-read as it lands (US-34 AC6, 2026-09-25). Before, a draft typed here outlived the erase, and was committed into the new record when the user started again. A matrix on screen when the erase arrives drops its own copy too, with what it lent the plan and the chat (round 4: the other device erased and started again before this page re-read, so the matrix stayed on screen, wrote the draft back on the next keystroke and committed it into the new record on the next leave). Known gap: a page that was closed through the erase keeps no memory of the record it had, so a draft left on it is not cleared by its next load. Since 2026-10-21 (orchestrator O5, D4 step 5, corrected twice the same day after review) one clear serves both: an erase taken in from another device clears what AC1 clears here, stored document originals (health_roadmap_doc_v2:*) included, except the original of a document that outlives the erase. The record session decides which (RecordSession.clearOffFileData): a document live in the record after the erase (added after it, or never seen by it: US-09 AC20, AC23), or live in the device's own record copy (the localStorage record a guest or on-device fallback tab writes) once the erase is applied to that copy, keeps its original; an original the erase listed goes even where a stale device copy still names it, and a device copy that cannot be read names nothing. An erase made here goes by the same rule on the device tier, and the page's own clear after an erase (HealthTool) goes through it too: the page never clears stored originals itself. Residual: a cloud-tier erase made here still removes the device record and every stored original with it (the mirror wipe), so a row, a document's included, that a guest or fallback tab of this browser saves after the erase read the device record is lost with it, as before. Tests: roadmap-store-remote-erase.test.ts (each off-file kind, by a re-read and by a save; tokens and consent keys kept); roadmap-store-erase-keeps-originals.test.ts (a stale guest tab keeps an original uploaded after the erase, by a re-read and a save, still readable; a cloud page keeps an on-device fallback tab's original; a listed original goes though a stale device copy names it; an unreadable device record names none; an orphan original goes; the page's erase keeps the original another tab saved while it ran and removes the erased one); record-session.session.test.ts (the keep set: a post-erase document, the device copy's unseen document but not its listed one, nothing from an unreadable copy).
  • AC7 (2026-09-25; an unreadable record now refuses the erase, and the time rule gave way to listed ids: US-09 AC23, 2026-10-20): an erase beats the erase and fresh start of a copy it had not seen, and reports success only once it is written. deleteUserData bumped eraseEpoch from its own copy alone, so a tab or device that had not seen another's erase and fresh start erased at an EQUAL epoch; the merge unioned the two, the other copy's new rows stayed, and the erase reported success. It now bumps past the stored epoch too, read at erase time. The read is a round trip on a cloud, and a save could start during it: its flush then answered at once beside the running save, the erase reported success and wiped the device mirror, and a tab closed before that save's second pass lost the erase. Now a flush made while a save runs joins it and answers when that save ends, extra passes included: a later edit's failed pass can make the erase report a failure it did not have, never a success it did not have. A save ends before it announces anything, so a listener that saves again starts a new save. The erase also drops a change still on the debounce instead of saving it first, since the erase throws it away. That also closes the older window while the reminders cancel and the chat-history erase ran first. A failed erase counts as unsaved, so the next hide retries it (US-10 AC5). Residuals: a write that lands between the epoch read and the save's own read can still meet the erase at an equal epoch and union; an epoch read that fails leaves this copy's epoch, so the save can land beside a newer erase, merge instead of winning, and still report success; and an erase in an on-device fallback session bumps past the device file only, not the cloud it cannot reach. Since US-09 AC20 (2026-10-20) the erase beats the other copy's fresh start by time as well as epoch: that copy's measurements, lab values and documents created at or after the erase's erasedAt survive it, and that is a wall-clock comparison across two devices. The erase-time floor (erasedAt is 1 ms past the latest updatedAt the eraser read, its own included) means every row the eraser had seen goes whatever its clock says; a row written after the epoch read, or stamped by a clock running ahead, can still survive. Found by the Codex review of US-10 AC5 and the adversarial review after it. Tests: roadmap-store-two-tabs.test.ts, the US-11 AC7 block (a stale tab and a stale device erase over another's erase and fresh start; success only once the erase is written, with a save running when it began; no save of the change the erase throws away; a flush made by a listener to a save that just ended starts a new save; an erase that failed to save is written by the next hide).
  • AC8 (2026-09-28, adversarial review): an erase empties the chat's copy of the record (health_roadmap_data, the copy the blog chat bubble and the chatbot embed read), and the embed on the page mutes.

- On this device: the erase clears the copy and tells the embed.

- From another device: this device empties its copy when the widget next loads here, or takes the erase in by a re-read.

- Known gap: until the widget loads on this device, the blog bubble and the embed here keep sending the pre-erase record with each chat message. A reply can quote it, and replies on those surfaces are kept for 30 days (US-15 AC8). A profile edit still waiting to save on the widget page also holds the clear until it saves. The privacy addendum's deletion paragraph says so.

- The server's copy (round 3, 2026-09-28): the Shopify confirm names six things the erase cannot reach. The sixth is the chat questions from the widget, the blog chat bubble and the chatbot embed, plus the bubble's and embed's replies, all kept on our server for 30 days (US-15 AC7, AC8). The alert after an erase repeats items 5 and 6 in short (AC5). The Pages build has none of these surfaces, so it keeps four items. The addendum says "Six copies". Tests: HealthTool.erase-copy.test.ts.

  • Tests: ✅ deleteUserData + stale-device-cannot-resurrect covered (2026-08-07). ✅ AC6: roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts ("clears both drafts when an erase made on another device arrives, by a re-read or by a save"; "clears the Lp(a) check's kept answers when an erase made on another device arrives, by a re-read or by a save") and HealthTool.journey.test.tsx (the page takes the erase in; starting again brings nothing back). ✅ Round 4: HealthTool.journey.test.tsx (a draft still on screen when the erase arrives: no keystroke brings it back, and a leave commits nothing) and roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts (a matrix on screen is told, by a re-read and by a save). ✅ 2026-09-25: HealthTool.journey.test.tsx (an erase made here takes back what both matrices' drafts lent: the plan and the chat read neither, and no draft is left on the device).
  • Incident 2026-08-07: first coverage of this path found that migrateFile() dropped meta.eraseEpoch on every storage read, so any stale device's flush resurrected erased data (merge gate never saw the epoch). Fixed in migrate.ts same day; regression tests pin it in roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts + sync-manager.test.ts.

US-29 · My AI agent reads and writes my record file directly — docs-only, 2026-09-01

As a user whose health record is one JSON file in my own cloud, I can point Claude Code or ChatGPT at it and have my agent read my history and append new results, because the format and the safety rules are published — not reverse-engineered.

  • AC1: docs/health-roadmap-file.schema.json is a draft 2020-12 JSON Schema for the record at schemaVersion 1 and 2 (2 once an erase has listed its rows, US-09 AC23), published at a stable raw-GitHub URL, and a record built through the real code paths (createEmptyFile → mergeFiles → migrateFile) validates against it; a malformed record fails.
  • AC2: docs/agent-access.md states where the file lives per backend, and matches the adapters (adapter.ts ROADMAP_FILE_NAME, dropbox.ts, drive.ts, github.ts) rather than restating folder names from memory.
  • AC3: The write rules are stated as hard rules — never mutate or delete a row; a correction appends a row with correctsId and flips the old row to entered-in-error (one-way); fresh UUID per row; meta.lamport/meta.eraseEpoch are off-limits; SI canonical units for measurements, the lab's own unit for lab values (superseded 2026-09-18: a catalogued lab test is stored in its SI unit, US-21 phase 3; an uncatalogued one still keeps the unit it was reported in); catalogue keys from lab-catalog.ts for metricName; never write fieldStamps on the profile or the screening answers, and to change a field by hand, move the object's updatedAt and leave its lamport (added 2026-09-25, US-10 AC6).
  • AC4: The honest caveats are stated — a filesystem write has no lock and no version guard, the app merges on its next sync, malformed rows are dropped or ignored rather than repaired.
  • AC4a: Migration omits a measurement or additional lab row whose recordedAt is not a string beginning with a real calendar day, before any slot or latest-value selection can read it. It never invents a clinical date. Valid date-only strings and timestamp prefixes, including their original zones and future days, remain unchanged. This checks the calendar-day prefix, not the timestamp suffix; it does not introduce a future-date eligibility policy. Omitted rows are absent from the record on a subsequent ordinary save: this is malformed-row normalization under AC4, not quarantine, and no recovery store is added. The read-only get-plan command does not rewrite the source file, including its malformed rows. Document addedAt is not rewritten: clamping it to each revision's own metadata anchor split identical document content and revived a deletion tombstone, so that clock repair is withdrawn, not solved. The app's own writers (bulkAppendValues, RoadmapStore.addMeasurement) refuse a recordedAt the reader would drop, so a save never fails its own readback. Unknown fields on retained rows survive, migration is deterministic for complete stored metadata, and legitimate post-erase rows still merge. This does not repair future document write clocks, self-consistent future file clocks, or erase rules. Tests: packages/health-core/src/migrate-stored-dates.test.ts, widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts and tools/get-plan.test.ts (US-30 AC5's hardened input boundary).
  • Usage signal (declared honestly, per the constitution): there is none from us, by design — the file is in the user's storage and reading or writing it contacts no server we own, so no product_events row can exist without breaking the promise. What we can watch instead: unprompted GitHub issues, stars, and traffic on the repo and the schema URL; and organic movement in the existing cloud funnel (cloud_connect_started/success), since an agent user needs a cloud backend first. Both are weak and lagging. If neither moves within a quarter, this stays a docs page and earns no code.
  • Tests: ✅ AC1 (roadmap-file.schema.test.ts — empty record, full merged record with a real entered-in-error correction pair, unknown-field forward-compat, malformed record, twelve per-invariant negative cases (two for field stamps, 2026-09-25), a representative record carrying field stamps, and an enum parity pin that deep-equals the schema's MetricType/MeasurementSource/medicationKey/document-type enums against validation.ts so drift breaks the build). ❌ AC2–AC4 are prose; nothing tests that the doc still matches the adapters — a folder rename would drift silently.

US-30 · My agent computes my actual plan, offline — added 2026-09-01

As a user whose record is one JSON file, I can run npx tsx tools/get-plan.ts ~/Dropbox/…/health-roadmap.json and get the same plan the web app would give me — current values, what's due, suggestions with reasons and citations — on my own machine, with no network call and no LLM. US-29 published the format so any agent can READ the file; this is the part only this repo can do: turn it into Brad's protocol.

  • AC1: get-plan <file> prints the plan — profile line, current key values (value + unit + clinical date), what's due, and suggestions grouped by priority with reason, guideline tags and citation URLs. The process opens no socket: the module graph is health-core + node builtins, nothing from app/ or widget-src/.
  • AC2: For the same record file the derived inputs and the resulting suggestion set are IDENTICAL to what the widget computes — same latestActivePerMetric → measurementsToInputs → calculateHealthResults path (US-07 AC4), asserted against a real RoadmapStore.loadLatestMeasurements() over a file built through the real code paths.
  • AC3: --json emits { instruction, schemaVersion, generatedAt, today, profile, inputs, unitSystem, medications, screenings, currentValues, labValues, due, suggestions, source } — stable field names, every current value and lab row carrying its id (what edit-record.ts correct --id takes), every suggestion carrying id/category/priority/reason/guidelines/references, so an agent can act on it without scraping prose. Documented in --help. Amended 2026-09-28 (US-07 AC5): currentValues prints LDL and ApoB on the side of their "<X" line the plan grades them (formatGradedValue), as the suggestion cards do, so LDL 1.40 mmol/L reads 55 mg/dL in both, not 54 in one and 55 in the other. Tests: packages/health-core/src/plan-current-values.test.ts.
  • AC4: --html <out> writes ONE self-contained file — inline CSS, no CDN, no script needed to read it — rendering the same plan for a human to keep or print.
  • AC5: The file is untrusted input: it is loaded through migrateFile, so the hardened second-writer boundary applies (US-10/US-29), and a missing file, unparseable JSON, a newer schemaVersion, or a record with no height/sex exits 1 with one plain line plus a hint — never a stack trace.
  • AC6: Read-only and silent: the tool never writes the record file, never mutates a row, never calls a model, and never emits telemetry. Health values reach stdout, or the --html file the user named, and nowhere else.
  • AC7 (start from numbers, 2026-10-20): get-plan --from-values <values.json | -> prints the same plan from numbers an agent has, with no record file. The JSON names sex, heightCm, age (or birthYear) and values (metric or test, value, unit, optional date). The record is built in memory through the writers edit-record uses (updateProfile, appendMeasurement, appendLabValue), so ranges, unit conversion and the one-value-per-day rule are theirs. A metric with two units (LDL mmol/L or mg/dL, HbA1c %, weight kg or lbs) with no unit, a value outside the app's range, a missing sex or height, or --from-values beside a record file exits 1 with one plain line plus a hint. Output (text, --json, --html) matches the file path; nothing is written, and no network call or telemetry is made.
  • Usage signal (declared honestly, per the constitution): none from us, by design — same as US-29, and for the same reason: the computation happens on the user's machine against their own file, so any event we could count would break the promise. What we can watch: Brad's own recurring use (user zero runs it from Claude Code against his real record), and unprompted outside interest — GitHub issues, stars, repo traffic. Both weak and lagging. If neither moves within a quarter this stays a tool for one user, and that is an acceptable outcome for a conviction bet.
  • Tests: ✅ tools/get-plan.test.ts — AC2 parity against the real store (deep-equal inputs + identical suggestion ids), AC3 JSON shape + parseability, AC4 self-contained HTML (no http(s):// script/link refs), AC5 all four error paths + a null-riddled file surviving migrateFile, AC1 static import guard (no app/, no widget-src/, no network module). ✅ AC7 (2026-10-20): same plan as the equivalent record file (text and --json), mg/dL conversion, missing unit refused, out-of-range and missing height/sex refused, a second value for one day refused, stdin - with nothing written to disk. ❌ Not tested: how the HTML looks in a browser (read by eye).

US-31 · My agent adds and corrects values in my record — added 2026-09-01

As a user whose record is one JSON file, I can run npx tsx tools/edit-record.ts add ~/Dropbox/…/health-roadmap.json --metric ldl --value 2.1 and have the value land in my file with the FHIR rules kept for me — one active value per metric per day, corrections that append instead of overwrite, a backup before every write — instead of hand-editing JSON and hoping. US-29 published the write rules and US-30 gave the read half; this is the code that enforces those rules, and the same code the hosted MCP server will call.

  • AC1 (altitude): the write operations are PURE FUNCTIONS in packages/health-core/src/record-edits.ts — appendMeasurement, appendLabValue, correctValue — each taking a RoadmapFile plus a request and returning a NEW file; the input is never mutated. Every rule below is enforced there, never in the CLI, so the CLI and the remote MCP server cannot drift apart.
  • AC2 (slot): appending into a (metric, calendar day) slot an active row already holds is REJECTED, not written — a typed rejection carrying that row (agent-access rule 3; mirrors RoadmapStore.addMeasurement's 409 semantics). Lab slots key on the catalogue key, so "Gamma GT" and ggt collide exactly as a lab import would.
  • AC3 (correction): correctValue appends a row with correctsId and the ORIGINAL recordedAt, then flips the corrected row to entered-in-error — a correction changes the value, never the date. It works on measurements and lab values, and rejects an id that is absent or already entered-in-error.
  • AC4 (range): a measurement outside healthInputSchema's range for that metric is rejected with the range in the message. Lab values carry no ranges, so they are accepted as the lab reported them.
  • AC5 (catalogue + units): metricName is stored as the lab-catalog.ts key whenever the test is catalogued (rule 10), and folded to lower case when it is not, so two spellings of one test share one slot. That resolution covers the spaced and Title-cased forms of a snake_case key — "Vitamin D" and "vitamin d" both file under vitamin_d — which is what an agent or a person actually types; the single labSlotKey() in lab-catalog.ts is the one place that key is computed, at write, merge and read time alike. value on a measurement is SI canonical (rule 8): the OPS resolve --unit through units.ts's reportedToCanonical — the same table (lookupUnit) the chatbot's proposed edits use, so the two writers cannot accept different spellings of one unit — and refuse anything else, so the CLI cannot mis-scale a value the MCP would scale correctly. A core metric written as a lab test is refused under every spelling in CORE_METRIC_ALIASES (its key, its display label, and the report spellings the extractor knows, such as "LDL-C", "A1C" and "Apo B"; amended 2026-10-14, PR #126 from Austin Bell), because a core metric in labValues is invisible to the suggestion engine. The refusal names the metric to write instead. Height is refused too and sent to update_profile (heightCm), since height lives in the profile.
  • AC6 (clocks + dates): every op moves meta.updatedAt to the write clock and touches no other meta field (rule 6), so the load clamp never rewinds the row just written — and it moves FORWARD only, as mergeFiles does, so a writer whose clock lags the file cannot rewind every other row's createdAt and hand the slot tie-breaks to a UUID comparison. recordedAt is refused if it is a day NO ONE has reached yet — the check is the latest calendar day anywhere on Earth (UTC+14), not the writing machine's own day, because an Auckland user's real today is tomorrow to a server in UTC and refusing it would be the server calling the user wrong. It is also refused if it is not a day that exists (2026-02-30 rolls forward in Date, so it is caught by round-trip), and is STORED as the calendar day — never the caller's string, so what is echoed back and what lands on disk are the same thing.
  • AC7 (no delete, v1 scope): there is no delete operation, and no medication, supplement or screening op — v1 writes clinical values only. Deletion stays what the app makes it (a document tombstone, or an eraseEpoch bump for everything), and neither is reachable from the CLI. The current-state rows are last-write-wins, so a second writer editing them needs the lamport discipline this v1 deliberately does not take on.
  • AC8 (safe write): the CLI backs the record up beside itself (health-roadmap.json.bak-<ISO>, the last 3 kept and older ones pruned), then writes atomically — temp file, then rename, keeping the record's own permissions rather than widening them to the umask default. It refuses to write anything that is not a record (valid JSON that is an array, a string or an object without schemaVersion would otherwise be replaced by a blank record), refuses a .bak sibling as a target, follows a symlink to the real file instead of replacing the link, and refuses to write at all if the file changed between being read and being replaced. It writes the record and its .bak siblings and nothing else; no network, no model, no telemetry. Strengthened 2026-09-01 by US-32, unified 2026-09-02: that write boundary is now packages/health-core/src/file-adapter.ts — a StorageAdapter over one local path — and the CLI writes through SyncManager over it, exactly as the hosted server writes through SyncManager over Dropbox. So there is ONE write path across all three shells, and the storage backend is chosen purely by which adapter SyncManager is handed. Two consequences: the changed-file guard is now a ConflictError that SyncManager answers by re-reading and re-MERGING (a second writer costs a retry rather than a refusal, and cannot cause a lost update), and the stale-bytes check is a content hash rather than mtime+size, so an equal-length edit inside the same millisecond is still caught. Made true 2026-09-02: that check and the replace it guards are held under a .lock sibling (O_EXCL, 25 ms backoff, 5 s wait), because a backup, a prune and a temp write sit between them — four concurrent edit-record PROCESSES used to keep one row and print "Wrote" four times. SyncManager's verify-after-write now also asserts every row id it just wrote is present on the re-read, so a writer that loses anyway reports it instead of confirming it. It also refuses a file that carries schemaVersion but holds junk where its rows belong (measurements, labValues, medications, supplements present but not a list) — migrateFile would have blanked such a file and the CLI would have reported success — and refuses a record written by a newer app at the READ, so it is out of reach in both directions. Moved 2026-09-02: that shape gate is ROADMAP_DOC.migrate (roadmap-doc.ts), not the adapter, so EVERY adapter inherits it — Dropbox, Drive, GitHub, the local file — on SyncManager.load() and on the re-read that precedes every save. A null or absent row array still normalises to []: it holds no rows, so nothing is lost. Lock hardening (2026-09-09): locks never expire solely by age. A suspended owner keeps its lock; publication/release verify its filesystem identity. Abandoned locks fail closed and require exclusive offline recovery with all writers terminated. This covers cooperative updated writers on one local filesystem, not legacy stealers or external lock replacement. Hardened again 2026-09-10 (late), five things the outside security read found in the same file. A backup made before the record's erase epoch is removed on the next write: an erase used to leave every pre-erase .bak sitting beside the erased file, which put "delete all my data" one rename away from undone; backups at or above the epoch are kept, because those are the user's ordinary undo, and a sibling the adapter cannot read as a record is left alone rather than guessed at. The temp file is opened exclusively under an unpredictable name and fsynced before the rename, so nobody can pre-plant it and a crash cannot leave a half-written record; a symlink planted at the temp or the backup path fails the write instead of being followed. Backup names carry no colon, so a Windows record can be saved at all. A record the tools create is 0600, and one left readable by everyone is narrowed rather than copied forward at that mode, the same rule US-33 AC5 applies to the HTML plan. And health-roadmap.json.* is now ignored in both .gitignore and .dockerignore, so a .bak, a .lock or a crashed .tmp cannot be committed or built into an image, the way US-09 AC9 already covers the record itself. Tests: packages/health-core/src/file-adapter.test.ts (the erase-epoch prune, the unreadable sibling, the never-erased record, the unpredictable temp name, the two planted symlinks, the colon-free backup name, 0600 on a fresh record and its backups, and the clamp on a world-readable one), tests/dockerignore.test.ts (the two ignore files stay in step).
  • AC9 (round-trip): bytes the CLI wrote load identically in the widget's own data layer — a real RoadmapStore over the written file reads the new value as current — and migrateFile plus a self-merge leave the file unchanged, because the edit is already canonical. Two devices that edit different slots from the same base both keep their edit through mergeFiles.
  • AC10 (errors): the same discipline as US-30 — exit 1 with one plain line plus a hint, never a stack; an occupied slot prints the row that holds it and how to correct it instead; a correction echoes old → new. Text out of the record reaches the terminal as data: control characters are stripped and newlines collapsed, so a lab name cannot forge a line of output that reads as the tool's own.
  • AC11 (today, per writer): "today" — the day a plan or a reminder measures against, and the default recordedAt where there is one — is the WRITER's own local calendar day. That works where the writer runs on the user's machine: the widget slots by the browser's local day and the CLI's --date defaults to the terminal's. It cannot work on the hosted server, and pretending otherwise was the bug (fixed 2026-09-03): a Fly box in UTC has no way to know an Auckland user's day, so a defaulted date was the UTC day and every user east of UTC was logged a day behind for part of their day. The hosted answer is not a better default but no default: recordedAt is REQUIRED on add_measurement and on every add_lab_values row, and the assistant — which does carry the user's date — passes the user's own local calendar day, asking if it does not know it. The schema is shared, so the stdio server asks for it too. get_plan's due-dates still measure against the server's day and can be a day out either way; that is cosmetic and is not fixed here. The time rule (Brad, 2026-10-21: "the database is always UTC, and then it's the user interface that actually shows the correct time zone"): moments (saved, uploaded, erased, every row stamp) are stored in UTC and shown in the user's time zone; calendar dates (a lab's collection date, the birth month, a screening date) are stored as the date itself, with no zone, and shown as written everywhere; "today", the day what is due is measured against, is the user's local calendar day, computed at display time. Server-side reminder maths uses UTC days until the user's time zone is stored (US-23 AC12). Tests: packages/health-core/src/plan-local-day.test.ts, packages/health-core/src/record-edits-local-day.test.ts, packages/health-core/src/reminder-schedule-local-day.test.ts, widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-local-day.test.ts, widget-src/src/lib/constants-local-day.test.ts.
  • Usage signal (declared honestly, per the constitution): none from us, by design — the same reason as US-29 and US-30. The edit happens on the user's machine against their own file; any event we could count would break the promise. What we can watch: Brad's own use as user zero, and unprompted outside interest (GitHub issues, stars, repo traffic). Weak and lagging. The one signal that would matter arrives later — whether the hosted MCP server, which reuses these functions, gets used at all.
  • Tests: ✅ packages/health-core/src/record-edits.test.ts (77: purity, slot rejection, correction date + status flip, out-of-range message, unit conversion incl. range-checking the CONVERTED value, US-32 · My AI assistant connects to my record — phase 0 shipped 2026-09-01; phase 1 LIVE 2026-09-02; phase 2 (Google Drive) LIVE 2026-09-02

As a user whose record is one JSON file, I can connect an AI assistant to it and say "add my new blood panel" or "what does my plan say about my LDL" — and it reads and writes my file by the app's own rules, because the tools are published by this repo rather than improvised by the model. Phase 0, shipped: a local stdio MCP server over a file path (Claude Desktop, Claude Code). Phase 1, LIVE at https://mcp.drstanfield.com/mcp: the same tools behind a hosted connector, so a web ChatGPT or Claude user clicks connect and reaches their Dropbox folder — the clunky step getting-started.md admits. The full architecture, and Brad's decisions on it verbatim, are in mcp-architecture.md (rev 4, decided 2026-09-01). Phase 2, LIVE 2026-09-02: the same server against Google Drive, offered on the consent screen beside Dropbox now that the GOOGLE_DRIVE_* secrets are set on health-tool-edu. Both items in deploy-runbook-mcp.md step 4b are now closed: Google brand verification is approved (the consent screen shows the branded "Dr Brad" screen, no "unverified app" interstitial), and the live verify over Drive (step 8) passed 2026-09-02 — the hosted MCP via Claude.ai wrote a measurement to the user's Drive file, the website loaded it, and a website correction was read back by Claude.

  • AC1 (one tool surface): the tools — read_record, get_plan, add_measurement, add_lab_values, correct_value, update_profile, report_feedback (seven at first; eight with import_documents, US-35; nine once file_results lands, US-36) — defined once in packages/health-core/src/mcp-tools.ts as pure functions over (file, request) with a Zod schema each, so the local server and the hosted one offer the same thing — the hosted surface exposes every tool in that list, with no hosted-only subset to drift. Reads and writes are separate tools by construction: no catch-all with a method argument.
  • AC2 (the file is untrusted input): every call reads the record fresh through migrateFile — the same hardened boundary US-29/US-30 use — so the assistant never works from a cached copy and a file another device changed mid-session is seen, not assumed.
  • AC3 (the capability secret never leaves): reminderOptIn.token is stripped from every read (agent-access rule 12). It manages the user's reminder schedule on Brad's server; an assistant has no use for it and a copy in a chat transcript is a copy that can cancel someone's reminders.
  • AC4 (writes keep the rules): every write goes through record-edits.ts (US-31 AC1–AC6) — one active row per (metric, day), SI canonical measurements, the lab's own unit for lab values (superseded 2026-09-18: a catalogued lab test is stored in its SI unit, US-21 phase 3; an uncatalogued one still keeps the unit it was reported in), catalogue keys, meta.updatedAt forward only. An add into an occupied slot is REJECTED and the refusal names the row holding the day and sends the agent to correct_value. add_lab_values is the lab-panel case: a batch, capped at 50 rows per call, all-or-nothing, so a half-imported panel never has to be told apart from a whole one.
  • AC5 (corrections are their own pathway): correct_value appends a row with correctsId and the ORIGINAL date and flips the old row to entered-in-error — never folded into an add. expectedValue — the agent stating what it believes it is replacing — is OPTIONAL on the local surface, where the user is watching their own file and the CLI has never asked for it, and REQUIRED on the hosted one, where it is what stops an agent writing from a stale or invented read. v1 writes clinical values only: no delete, and no medication, supplement, screening or document write, because those are last-write-wins current state a second writer can overwrite. Reversed for the profile on 2026-09-02 (US-34), for four fields and no others: update_profile changes sex, birth year, birth month and height — what the plan is computed from — as a read-modify-write of the whole last-write-wins profile object, so every field it does not name survives, unitSystem and any field a newer app added included. It refuses what the app itself would refuse (healthInputSchema's own ranges, and the same male/female enum), refuses a call naming no field, and refuses a wrong expected without disclosing what the record holds. On the hosted surface expected is REQUIRED for every field being changed (null claims the field is unset) and the write costs a correction's weight — 5 — because a profile field has no superseded copy to read back. Display preferences (unitSystem, unitOverrides) stay out of reach: they are how the app draws the screen, not what the record says about the person.
  • AC6 (the bytes): every surface writes through SyncManager over a StorageAdapter — read, migrate, merge, conditional write on expectedVersion, verify. The stdio server and the CLI hand it FileAdapter (packages/health-core/src/file-adapter.ts, one local path: backup, atomic replace, symlink target, content-hash precondition); the hosted server hands it the Dropbox adapter. What counts as a record at all is ROADMAP_DOC (roadmap-doc.ts), above the adapters, so every backend refuses the same bytes. The three shells are literally the same few lines — runToolOverSync in mcp-tools.ts — so they cannot lose the file in different ways, and the database of record is a constructor argument. A storage failure is worded once, by describeStorageFailure, and reaches the agent as a refusal on its own request rather than a protocol error it cannot match.
  • AC7 (zero network, phase 0): the local server speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio and opens no socket — the imports of the server, the tool layer, the plan engine and the local FileAdapter are pinned by a guard to health-core sources, their siblings, zod and node builtins. No hosting, no OAuth, no key, and the product promise is untouched.
  • AC8 (get_plan presents honestly): the plan JSON carries a top-level instruction telling the model to keep each suggestion's hedged wording as written and keep the references attached to the suggestion they belong to. The thresholds, reasons and citations are unchanged — get_plan re-exposes existing derivations, so the three-file rule is not triggered.
  • AC9 (the assistant files a bug report): report_feedback turns a complaint into a GitHub issue on this repo. On the hosted server the assistant files it itself, with no user action — a POST to the GitHub issues API under a server-held fine-grained token (GITHUB_ISSUES_TOKEN), titled [connector] <title>, labelled from-connector plus bug or enhancement, and answering { filed: true, url, number }. The report's text is fenced in the issue body, so a model's markdown renders as written and an @name pings nobody; the footer carries the kind, the server version, the cloud provider and one line saying the user's assistant filed it and no health values are included. Nothing identifies the user: no name, no email, no IP, no connection key. The issue is PUBLIC, and the tool description says so. A server with no token — always the local stdio server, which holds no secret — keeps the old behaviour: a prefilled issues/new?labels=from-connector,<bug|feature> URL, { filed: false }, which the user opens, reads and submits themselves; an over-long one is refused rather than silently truncated by GitHub. Keeping health values out is the tool description's job, and the mechanical backstop is the LAST line of defence, since nobody reviews a hosted report before it is public. Widened 2026-09-10, after a ChatGPT audit of the public repo found "My LDL is 3.2" and "I have HIV. Contact synthetic@example.invalid" both passing: a title or detail is refused as health-value when it carries a number wearing a known unit ("2.1 mmol/L", "81 kg", "140 mmHg", read off units.ts) OR a bare number within three words of a name this record knows, read off METRIC_LABELS and LAB_CATALOG so a metric added tomorrow joins the guard for free (single letters go — "k" is a thousand before it is potassium — as do the generic English words a test name is built from, "total", "count", "rate", and six short names that are English or markup first: na, gt, am, oh, sat, hs. Short names that are not stay, so "BP 140/90" and "free T4 15" are refused; "Lp(a)" is folded to one word on both sides so "my Lp(a) is 90" is too; and "the chart shows the wrong unit for HbA1c", a metric name with no number, still files). A second, new reason, contact, refuses an email address, a phone-shaped run of 7–15 digits (calendar days and timestamps masked out first) and a URL carrying a query string, which may carry a token. There is deliberately NO diagnosis word list: that cannot be done mechanically, and the description carries what the guard cannot — "This files a public GitHub issue. Do not include diagnoses, names, contact details, or values; describe the behaviour, not the person." The guard over-refuses rather than under: a refused report is rephrased in a turn, a filed one is public forever. Because it now writes to an external system the tool is no longer read-only (readOnlyHint: false, openWorldHint: true) and costs a correction's five against the connection's hourly write allowance — charged before the call, so a refusal spends too, exactly as correct_value does. Two more bounds live on the server: at most 20 issues an hour across the whole machine (over that, "Feedback is paused for an hour. Nothing was filed."), and the same title filed twice in 24 hours returns the first issue's URL instead of a second issue. A third bound is per connection: three reports in a rolling 24 hours (over that, "You have filed three reports today. Nothing was filed." — and, like every refusal here, it still spends the write allowance), and the GitHub call itself is abandoned after 8 seconds, which lands in the same "GitHub did not answer" refusal. A GitHub failure is worded as ours — "GitHub did not answer. Nothing was filed. Try again later." — never a protocol error, and the log line carries the status and not a word of the report. It still opens no cloud connection: RECORD_FREE_TOOLS runs it before any record is loaded, which is the point — the likeliest moment to report a bug is the moment the record would not open. Amended 2026-09-11: the fence protects the BODY, and the title had nothing. unsafeFeedback does not catch a bare @handle, and loop-issue-notify.yml relays a from-connector issue (authored under Brad's own PAT, so it passes that workflow's author check) by interpolating ${issue.title} RAW inside … in a public comment — where GitHub links @name, #123, owner/repo#1, text and a bare https:// on sight. So an assistant-chosen title could ping a stranger, post a reference event in someone else's repository, or render a live phishing link in a bot comment on a doctor's public repo. titleSafe now puts a zero-width space after every character that can start one of those, applied to the assistant's words only (our [connector] prefix stays clean) and after the length cap is taken off the raw title, so the cap can never cut between a character and its escape. _ is deliberately not on the list: it opens nothing but italics and every tool here is named with one. Fixed at the authoring layer rather than in the relay, because .github/workflows/** is Brad-only and the source fix covers every consumer of a title. Tests: mcp-tools.test.ts (mentions, a cross-reference, a Markdown link and a bare URL all inert; a plain title byte-identical; and the ordering case that fails if the escape is ever moved ahead of unsafeFeedback, where @​ would split an address past the email regex).
  • Usage signal (declared honestly, per the constitution): none from us, by design — phase 0 runs on the user's machine against their own file, so any event we could count would break the promise, exactly as for US-29/30/31. What we can watch: Brad's own use as user zero, and unprompted outside interest (GitHub issues, stars, repo traffic). Weak and lagging. Phase 1 is where a real signal first exists — a hosted connector is a request to our server, so connection and tool-call counts become countable without any health value in them; that measurement is designed with phase 1, not before. Built 2026-09-03: two product_events rows and nothing else — mcp_connect when a connection is granted (carrying which storage provider and which assistant, from a closed enum, never the client's own self-declared id) and mcp_tool_call per call (which tool, which assistant, whether it succeeded). No value, no metric name, no row id, no identifier, and nothing that links two calls to one person. Read against the connector guides' page views: if mcp_connect stays at zero, the guides are not landing; if it rises and mcp_tool_call does not, the connection is being made and not used. Stated plainly because it is true: while the user count is tiny, a timestamped row is value-free but not person-free — it can still be Brad's.
  • Phase 1 (LIVE — the honest status): deployed on health-tool-edu at https://mcp.drstanfield.com/mcp on 2026-09-02, with the Fly secrets set and the certificate issued. Dropbox only; the Dropbox app is approved for 500 users. Google Drive is a separate stream, not shipped. The kill switch is unsetting MCP_SEAL_KEYS, which returns every /mcp path and both .well-known documents to 404. Operator steps and the rotation procedure: deploy-runbook-mcp.md. Architecture and Brad's decisions verbatim: mcp-architecture.md.
  • Phase 1 evidence, 2026-09-02 first live connections: ChatGPT connected via CIMD (https://chatgpt.com/oauth/client.json) and read the record and the plan against a real Dropbox record; Claude's CIMD document is Cloudflare-challenged from Fly (403, cf-mitigated: challenge) → both canonical vendor ids are now pinned in KNOWN_CLIENTS (this commit), consulted before any fetch, with the fetch policy unchanged for unknown ids. Both vendors then connected end to end the same day against a real Dropbox record: Claude by Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector, and ChatGPT by Settings → Security → Developer mode → Plugins → Create app with Authentication OAuth. The guides now point at the live connector rather than promising one: getting-started.md's buttons went from greyed "coming soon" to links into step lists on the page, with the server address in a copy box; connect-chatgpt.md is new; connect-claude-desktop.md's "Claude on the web cannot do this" section is now the web steps. No vendor exposes a deep link that adds a connector on the reader's behalf; Anthropic documents one that PREFILLS the Add custom connector dialog for the user to confirm, and that is what the Claude steps use. OpenAI has no equivalent, and a ChatGPT user needs developer mode until the app is published through OpenAI's review — the requirements for that, and for an Anthropic directory listing, are in deploy-runbook.md "Publishing the ChatGPT app", unstarted and Brad's to do. Connector funnel (product-health): W36 3 connects; W37 0 and W38's first five days 0 — OpenAI's reviewer failed the OAuth flow some time 09-02 → 09-15 (v1.0.0 rejected 2026-09-15; attempt time unknown) and the old code counted no failures, so no window shows it; AC34's counters live 09-17: W38 authorize_shown 19 → refused 3 (resource 2, redirect-uri 1) → consent 7 → connect 5 + token-dead-code 1. v1.0.1 resubmitted (receipt 2026-09-17T20:30Z; #60). W39: shown 5 (codex 4 / claude 1) → consent 2 → connect 2 (dropbox via codex; google-drive via claude — the first Drive connect from Claude); no chatgpt row; no v1.0.1 verdict — OpenAI's 09-23 reply on the v1.0.0 thread says the reviewer stopped at the cloud sign-in for want of reviewer credentials.
  • AC10 (nothing per user is stored, anywhere): no table, no row, no session. (One exception, AC38: the refresh token for the one invented reviewer account, shared by OpenAI's and Anthropic's reviewers since AC49, is a server secret, and its sessions carry none.) The Dropbox refresh token is sealed into the bearer token the AI vendor holds — AES-256-GCM under a per-blob-type HKDF key, a 12-byte nonce, AAD binding the blob to one client and one audience, and fixed-bucket padding so the blob's length says nothing about the credential inside. We hold the key and no blob; the vendor holds a blob and no key. What DOES exist and is counted, not hidden: a per-machine authorization-code set, per-IP rate maps, a bounded client-metadata cache, and Fly's own proxy metadata. None is health data and none is a per-user row. What sealing does NOT protect: the blob the vendor holds is a live bearer against /mcp until it expires — no key needed. Split custody protects the DROPBOX credential inside it, not access to our endpoint.
  • AC11 (revocation is honest about what it cannot do): the access blob expires in 1 hour and the refresh blob in 90 days. Rotating MCP_SEAL_KEYS with no overlap kills every connection at once, and that is our ONLY server-side revocation — a per-user denylist needs state we refuse to keep. (One exception, AC38: the invented OpenAI reviewer account's sessions end when its reviewer secrets are unset or rotated.) The real kill switch is the user's own: dropbox.com/account/connected_apps. Because Dropbox's app-folder scoping is tied to the app identity, unlinking there ALSO disconnects this website from the folder; that is disclosed on the consent screen, not hidden.
  • AC12 (the four mandatory corrections mitigations): expectedValue is REQUIRED on the hosted surface (optional on the CLI and the local server); a correction on a row older than 90 days is refused; add_lab_values is capped at 50 rows per call; and writes are bounded at 60 weighted writes per connection per hour, per machine, where a correction costs five adds. The allowance is keyed on the connection (the hash of the sealed provider refresh token), so minting extra access tokens buys no extra writes, and it comes back with the hour, so an honest user is never locked out. Corrected 2026-09-02 by review: the approved design put a lifetime pool inside the credential, spent by refreshing. It locked honest users out — fifty ordinary refreshes with zero writes exhausted it — and bounded nobody, because replaying one refresh blob mints a fresh access blob every time. It is deleted. The honest bound is a RATE, per machine, and the refusal now says so.
  • AC13 (the accepted residual, stated rather than softened): an injected agent reads first, so it knows every row id and value, and with correct_value it can silently falsify current values — each original flipping to entered-in-error, irreversibly — and get_plan will then generate a coherent, wrong protocol from the falsified record. Append-only prevents data LOSS, not data CORRUPTION. Brad accepted this knowingly on 2026-09-01, choosing protocol completeness, bounded by AC11. Vendor confirmation prompts are NOT counted as a boundary: the MCP spec calls annotations untrusted hints and "always allow" is one click.
  • AC14 (state comes back byte-identical): state is the client's own opaque value, so it is returned byte-identical up to 1024 characters; longer is refused with invalid_request, never truncated. We used to .slice(0, 512) it. OpenAI's platform relay sends 521 characters, got a 512-character stump echoed back on the callback, and rejected every ChatGPT connection with "Invalid OAuth state" — a truncated state is worse than a missing one, because it looks valid until the far end compares it. The cap is set by the __Host-mcp-state cookie rather than by taste: the sealed state is padded to a fixed bucket, and 1024 keeps the whole Set-Cookie line near 3.1 KB, inside the 4096 bytes browsers allow, where the next bucket up would put it at ~5.8 KB and the browser would drop the cookie in silence. Twice what OpenAI sends, and more than Claude does.
  • AC14 (the front door): OAuth 2.1 with PKCE S256 only, our own consent screen — and the consent screen is ENFORCED, not merely displayed: pressing Connect mints a 32-byte nonce, seals the state naming it into a first-party __Host-mcp-state cookie (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, 30 minutes), and hands Dropbox the nonce alone. Amended 2026-09-16: that budget was 10 minutes and it starts when the consent screen PAINTS, not when Connect is pressed — sealState stamps exp at the authorize GET and the consent POST re-seals without restamping. Ten minutes had to cover reading the screen, signing in at the provider, creating an account if you have none, clearing the provider's device check, and returning; overrunning it renders a 400 on our own domain with no way back to the assistant. Lengthening it costs nothing, and not for the reason it looks like: the authorize GET is unauthenticated and mints a fresh state on demand, so this lifetime never bounded an attacker who wanted one. What bounds the flow is the cookie, the 32-byte nonce, PKCE, and the 60-second single-use code, and the blob itself carries no credential. The cookie's Max-Age is now derived from the same constant rather than retyped beside it. Two more front-door defects were fixed the same day, both found while investigating OpenAI's 2026-09-15 rejection ("We're unable to complete your sign-in or OAuth flow"): ChatGPT's pin carried one of the two callbacks in ALLOWED_REDIRECTS, and a pinned client is refused any redirect its own entry omits — answered NON-redirectably, so ChatGPT got a dead window rather than an error, live from the first hosted-MCP commit until now; and RFC 8707 resource was compared byte-exactly, so a client that normalised its own trailing slash, or named the issuer rather than the resource, was told this server is not that resource. Tests: mcp-auth.server.test.ts (the state clock runs from the GET; a pinned vendor can use every allow-listed redirect on its own host — the direction the old subset test could not see), mcp.hosted.test.ts (both ChatGPT callbacks accepted, a same-host unregistered path still refused, every spelling of our own audience accepted and no other). The callback requires the cookie, compares the echoed value to the sealed nonce timing-safely, and clears it; without the cookie it is a 400 page and no redirect. (Before this, found by review 2026-09-02, a state blob from an unauthenticated GET /mcp/authorize could be replayed into a forged callback and mint an authorization code with no consent at all.) Then RFC 8707 audience validation, RFC 9207 iss, and invalid_grant on every dead grant. The refresh lifetime is 90 days ABSOLUTE from consent — it used to slide forward on every refresh, so it expired for nobody. Clients arrive by client-id metadata document or by a self-contained DCR client id carrying its own HMAC — no registry, no row. The metadata fetch is an SSRF surface and is treated as one: https only, every resolved address public, zero redirects, a 5-second timeout, a 64 KB cap, application/json required, no credentials, and per-IP rate limiting BEFORE the fetch. Unauthenticated calls get 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="…"; the only unauthenticated documents are the two .well-known files.
  • AC15 (it is not a browser endpoint): no Access-Control-Allow-Origin is ever emitted, ALLOWED_ORIGINS is untouched, a present-but-foreign Origin gets 403, and localhost is on no list. GET and DELETE at the endpoint are 405, no Mcp-Session-Id is ever minted, and an incoming one — like Last-Event-ID — is ignored. No route logs a request URL, because code, state and code_verifier travel in query strings.
  • AC16 (consistency is the widget's, not a second implementation): every write goes through the same SyncManager read → migrate → merge → conditional-write → verify loop the widget runs, now living in health-core so both surfaces share it. The Dropbox conditional write sends strict_conflict, which is what stops a stale write re-creating a record the user erased. A record whose schemaVersion is newer than this server understands is out of reach in BOTH directions: the record is migrated before any tool sees it, so reads refuse too, and the refusal says so rather than claiming the record is readable. Known residual, unchanged from US-11: a RAW deletion in the Dropbox UI carries no eraseEpoch signal, so a stale writer legitimately re-creates the content.
  • AC17 (bounded, and honest when it refuses): request bodies are capped — 64 KB at the OAuth doors, 1 MB at /mcp, 413 over. /token is rate-limited per IP and tools/call per connection, both generously: a whole vendor's users arrive from one egress range, so a tight per-IP limit would lock out honest traffic rather than an attacker. The IP those limiters key on is Fly-Client-IP, which Fly's proxy writes, not X-Forwarded-For, which a client can forge. A malformed MCP_SEAL_KEYS or MCP_CLIENT_HMAC_KEY disables the feature (404) with one log line naming the variable and never its value, rather than turning every route into a 500. A record written by a NEWER app version refuses reads as well as writes — it is migrated before any tool sees it — and the refusal says that rather than claiming the record is readable. A failure that is ours, not the record's and not the provider's, reaches the client as JSON-RPC -32603 on the request's own id, never worded as a refusal the user could act on, on the hosted and the local server alike.
  • Known spec deviation, documented not papered over: OAuth 2.1 requires single-use authorization codes and statelessness cannot enforce that across Fly machines. The per-machine set is best-effort; the window is 60 seconds, and redemption still needs the PKCE code_verifier, which never leaves the client.
  • AC18 (phase 2 — the user picks the cloud, and the token remembers): the consent screen offers one button per configured provider, each carrying its own sealed state, so the choice is made before the browser leaves us and cannot be edited afterwards. provider lives INSIDE the sealed state, code, access and refresh payloads, under the same AES-256-GCM tag as the credential — so a Dropbox connection cannot be steered into opening a Drive folder, or the reverse, and an edited token dies rather than changing clouds. /mcp builds its adapter from the bearer token alone; no tool argument ever names a provider, a file or a user.
  • AC19 (phase 2 — Drive without a conditional write): Drive v3 has no etag, so DriveAdapter (packages/health-core/src/drive-rest.ts) substitutes the four steps of mcp-architecture.md §7 — read with fields=version, re-fetch the version immediately before uploading and refuse if it moved, verify every written row id on the re-read, and retry, bounded. Step 3 is SyncManager's existing verify-after-write, not a second implementation, and a failed verify is now a RETRYABLE lost update rather than a dead end; when the retries run out the message says some of the change may have landed, which is the truth. Stated residual: the pre-upload check narrows the window, it does not close one. Probed 2026-09-10 against a scratch account, so this is not re-litigated: Drive v3 returns no ETag anywhere (fields=etag is 400 Invalid field selection, no ETag header on the metadata or media GET) and answers 200 to a media PATCH and a metadata PATCH carrying If-Match: garbage-etag. There is no conditional write on Drive v3; check-then-act plus verify-after-write plus bounded retry is the strongest sequence the API allows. The browser adapter did not check versions at all until 2026-09-09 (US-10 AC4); it now runs the same check, and the residual on both sides is the one-PATCH check-to-upload gap. Discovery of the folder (Health Plan by Dr Brad) and the record inside it lives once in health-core and is called by both the browser adapter and the server: two implementations would give a user two records and show them neither whole.
  • AC20 (phase 2 — Google is off until the console work is done): the Google leg reuses the OAuth client the widget already uses (GOOGLE_DRIVE_CLIENT_ID/GOOGLE_DRIVE_SECRET), because drive.file shows an app only the files that app created and a second identity would open an empty Drive. Scope is drive.file and nothing else; access_type=offline with prompt=consent, and no include_granted_scopes. A provider with no secrets is not offered, so merging phase 2 changed nothing for anyone until Brad set the two Fly secrets. Done 2026-09-02 (deploy-runbook-mcp.md step 4b): the redirect URI https://mcp.drstanfield.com/mcp/callback is registered, publishing status is In production — in "Testing", Google expires every refresh token after 7 days and every connection breaks at once with no server-side remedy — and the secrets are set on health-tool-edu. Brand verification for drive.file approved 2026-09-02: the consent screen shows the branded "Dr Brad" screen, no unverified-app interstitial. The cost, stated: Google caps refresh tokens at 100 per account per client id, shared with the widget; each connection mints one, and past the cap Google silently drops the oldest, which can be the website's own.
  • AC21 (loopback redirects, so a command-line client can connect — added 2026-09-02): a redirect whose scheme is http and whose host is exactly 127.0.0.1, [::1] or localhost is accepted on ANY port, provided the client registered a loopback redirect with the same host, path and query — the port is the one part a CLI cannot know until it binds a listener (RFC 8252 §7.3). https://localhost and any non-loopback http stay refused, at registration and at /authorize; the host is matched exactly, so localhost.evil.com and 127.0.0.1.evil.com are ordinary public names and get nothing; userinfo and a fragment are refused outright. One helper, redirectMatches(registered, requested) in app/lib/mcp-clients.server.ts, is the only comparison, used at /authorize and at /token. PKCE S256 stays mandatory — the code that reaches a loopback port is worthless without the verifier — and the consent screen still names the client before anything is granted. Claude Code's own metadata document (https://claude.ai/oauth/claude-code-client-metadata) is Cloudflare-challenged from Fly like the web one, so it is pinned in KNOWN_CLIENTS with the two loopback redirects it publishes; Gemini CLI registers dynamically.
  • AC22 (update_profile, and why it is a tool at all — added 2026-09-03; the tool shipped 2026-09-02 without an AC): an assistant can change four things about the user — sex, birth year, birth month, height — because a plan cannot be computed without them and asking the user to leave the chat and open the app to type their height is where the connector stops being useful. They are current-state scalars, not clinical rows: there is no superseded copy and no history, so last-write-wins is the whole model and losing one silently is the risk. The guard is therefore the same shape as a correction's: expected is REQUIRED per field being changed, a claim about one field is not a claim about another, and a mismatch is refused without echoing what the record actually holds. It costs five adds, like correct_value, and a REFUSED attempt spends the cost too — otherwise an agent could learn a user's height by guessing at it for free. A change to a field the caller did not name leaves that field alone, and since 2026-09-25 so does the merge: the tool stamps only the fields it changes, and each field is last-write-wins on its own (US-10 AC6).
  • AC23 (report_feedback files it, and says what that means): on the hosted server the assistant files a PUBLIC GitHub issue on this repo under a server-held token, with no user action — so the user's words leave their machine and become public the moment they ask. That is disclosed on the consent screen, in the guides and in the tool's own description, never only in the code. What is sent is the title, the report text (fenced, so its markdown is text and cannot forge the footer) and the server version; no health values, no record contents, no identifier. It is capped at 20 an hour across the server and 3 a day per connection, and an identical report inside the window is deduplicated rather than filed twice. The mechanical guard (AC9) refuses a value, an email address, a phone number or a link with a query string before anything is prepared. The stdio server holds no token: it prepares a prefilled GitHub link, answers filed: false, and files nothing.
  • AC28 (the assistant is told the code is open, added 2026-09-09): the server instructions end with one sentence naming the repository, saying the project is open source and MIT licensed, and saying report_feedback is how to propose a change. Both servers say it, from one exported constant, so the hosted and stdio surfaces cannot drift; the repository itself is named once, in plan.ts, and every URL that points at the code derives from it, including the schema URL and report_feedback's own filing target. get_plan's source block gains repo, because without it the tool and docs paths beside it are file names an assistant cannot open. Why it matters: an assistant that knows the code is readable can answer "is this safe?" with the source rather than a promise, and can read what a tool actually does before reporting it. Usage signal: the volume of from-connector issues, already watched by the product-health loop.
  • AC29 (a refusal says why, value-free, added 2026-09-09): mcp_tool_call carries a reason when, and only when, the outcome is refused. The vocabulary is closed and lives beside the other counter vocabularies: the record layer's own eleven EditRejectionReason members, which it already decided and until now threw away, plus the surface's own — malformed, too-old (the 90-day rule), allowance, confirm, health-value, no-record, import (whose detail is on the mcp_import row) and other. A word the list does not name is dropped and counted as other, so free text can never enter a counter, and a compile-time check in mcp-tools.ts stops the two vocabularies drifting. No value, date, row id, unit or file name can reach the field. Why: "refused" alone says a user hit a wall and not which wall, and the walls are where the product is wrong. Usage signal: the reason breakdown itself, weekly.
  • AC30 (Codex is a named client, not other, added 2026-09-09): OpenAI's command-line agent connects with codex mcp add health --url https://mcp.drstanfield.com/mcp and codex mcp login health. It asks by client-id metadata document — https://chatgpt.com/oauth/codex/client.json, client_name "Codex", loopback redirects — not by DCR, so before this it resolved through the fetch path and every counter row said other. It is pinned in KNOWN_CLIENTS with its own codex label, which buys the same two things the other pins buy: a counter that can tell Codex from an unknown client, and immunity to the day Cloudflare decides our datacenter is a bot, as it already did to claude.ai (AC21). Its redirects are the loopback pair it publishes, so the port it binds at login varies and nothing else does. The ChatGPT connector's own web callback and Codex's loopback stay separate identities: neither can borrow the other's redirect. Usage signal: mcp_connect and mcp_tool_call rows carrying client: 'codex'.

  • AC24 (a website upload never silently loses a value to a connector row — added 2026-09-03): when an uploaded lab report carries a number for a (metric, day) an active row already holds, the review table shows the CONFLICT — what the record holds, what the document says, and a Replace checkbox that is UNCHECKED by default — instead of dropping the document's number before the user ever sees it. Equal values are not a conflict and stay as context. Replacing is a correction and is written as one: the old row flips to entered-in-error, the new row carries correctsId and the ORIGINAL date. Nothing auto-supersedes on source rank: a correction asserts the old value was WRONG, and only the person can assert that.

Each suggestion also carries its link, the one field the tool layer used to drop.
  • AC26 (read_record returns what was asked for): with a metric filter set, the answer carries no documents[] — a filter is a request for one metric, and shipping the whole document list with it spends the client's context on something the caller did not ask for. That lab row is not the plan's value; the measurement is.
