  • AC34 (the front door counts its own refusals — added 2026-09-17): OpenAI's reviewer was refused at /mcp/authorize for two weeks and nothing recorded it. The only trace was a console.error, and Sentry drops the Console integration on purpose; Fly's log buffer is half an hour deep. mcp_connect fires on a completed callback alone, so a funnel reading zero said "nobody connected" and "everybody was refused" in the same words. Usage signal (declared, Lane B): four server-only product_events rows over the whole OAuth door — mcp_authorize_shown {client} when the consent page renders, mcp_authorize_refused {client, reason} on every exit from the authorize GET, mcp_consent_posted {client, provider} when the user presses Connect, and mcp_connect_failed {client?, provider?, reason} on every later exit that never reaches a code. Read as a funnel: shown → posted → connect is the honest denominator mcp_connect never had, and a refused count that rises while shown does not is a vendor being turned away — the exact shape of the two weeks nobody could see. reason is a closed word from MCP_OAUTH_REASONS naming the CHECK that failed (unknown-client, redirect-uri, rate-limited, nonce-mismatch, exchange-failed, and the rest), never the value that failed it: a redirect_uri, a client_id and a state are all caller-chosen text, and none of them reaches a row. checkAuthorize returns that word itself rather than an English description the route would have to read back. The console.error stays — it names the client's host, which a closed vocabulary cannot. Extended 2026-09-17: /token was the last blind spot — it wrote no row on any path, so a client that was shown the screen, pressed Connect and came back from the provider could still fail to become a token with nothing to show for it. Every exit there now writes mcp_connect_failed with the check that failed (token-bad-request, token-grant-type, token-dead-code, token-client, token-redirect, token-pkce, token-replayed, token-dead-refresh), because the endpoint deliberately answers one invalid_grant to every dead grant and the counter is the only place the difference may be said. Same change: an empty resource= is treated as absent rather than as a foreign audience, because a client that serialises every parameter it knows should not be refused over punctuation.
  • AC35 (a read says what its numbers are in — added 2026-09-18, from a Hermes agent's review of the connector, reported on Discord): a bare number is a guess, and a guessed unit is a wrong health value. Both reads now state the contract in-band. read_record carries a units map keyed by metricType, the way its rows are keyed; get_plan carries one keyed by the inputs field name (weightKg: 'kg', apoB: 'g/L', heightCm: 'cm'), the way ITS payload is keyed. Both are built from UNIT_DEFS, so a new metric joins without a second list to maintain. The read_record description, the PLAN_SECTIONS descriptions for inputs and profile, and one shared SI_NOTE sentence in the instructions of BOTH servers say the same thing, so an assistant is told at connect and again per tool. Three things the map does not cover, said in words instead: labValues[].unit is the lab's own string, unconverted (superseded 2026-09-18: a catalogued lab test is stored in its SI unit, US-21 phase 3; an uncatalogued one still keeps the unit it was reported in); get_plan.inputs is SI canonical while currentValues is the same values converted to the record's unitSystem; and a metric off the catalogue has no canonical unit at all.
  • AC36 (a thin plan says why it is thin — added 2026-09-18, same review): creatinine joins GATING_INPUTS, so a record without one is told in missingInputs that this is why eGFR is null and why the protein target carries no CKD adjustment — five gating markers now, not four. profile.waistToHeightRatio is in the payload beside bmiCategory, and the profile description says the category is waist-informed (a BMI of 25–29.9 with a ratio below 0.5 reads Normal, AACE 2025 / NICE), so a reader is not left explaining a number that disagrees with the BMI it can compute. And the plan's floor is stated and tested: on a record holding no measurement at all, protein-target, exercise and sleep rest on no value whatever (the test pins those three, and that a lipid card is absent), the screening, skin and supplement cards follow from sex and age alone, and fiber shows whenever lipids are not elevated, absent lipids included, so it means "no lipid card", never "lipids fine". Every other suggestion is conditional on a measurement, which is how an assistant tells a thin plan from a clean bill of health.

The suggestion wording is untouched, so the three clinical files are too. read_record surfaces no suggestion links: the one place a record could hold them, recommendationSnapshots, has no writer. Restoring all three is that one edit. This amends AC28 for as long as the flag stands. A GitHub failure of any kind (silence, a 5xx, or a refusal such as a flagged account's 403) now reads "Feedback could not be filed right now. Nothing was posted. Try again later.", amending AC9's "GitHub did not answer", which was false when GitHub answered and refused. An address in the well-known NAT64 prefix 64:ff9b::/96 (RFC 6052) is judged by the IPv4 address it carries, so a DNS64 answer for a public host passes: 64:ff9b::101:101 and 64:ff9b::1.1.1.1 (1.1.1.1) pass, while 64:ff9b::7f00:1 and 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe are refused, hex and dotted spellings alike (maintainer commit, 2026-10-19, plan option 2). A public address in the standard mapped prefix stays allowed, including the hex spelling ::ffff:0101:0101, which the old remainder check refused. A public address written with a trailing dotted quad stays allowed. A string that starts with fc or fd, or with ::ffff: but is not the mapped prefix, stays refused. An address the check cannot parse is refused. Teredo was not classified here; AC47 now refuses it with the rest of 2001::/23.   • AC47 (2026-10-19, follow-up to AC45): a client-metadata fetch connects only to an address it checked. It uses Node's https.request with its own lookup: every address the name resolves to must be public or the connection fails, and the socket goes to an address from that same answer, so a DNS-rebinding resolver gets no second look. Node calls no lookup for an IP-literal host, so a literal is checked before any request, brackets stripped; a public literal is fetched as before. The fetch's agent keeps no TLS session (maxCachedSessions: 0) and no keep-alive, so a session ticket an attacker's server issued cannot ride a later connection to an internal address ("TLS poison"). What fetch did stays: one 5-second deadline over the whole request, body read included; every non-2xx refused, 3xx included, so no redirect is followed; a gzip, deflate or br body is decoded (x-gzip too), with the 64 KB cap checked on content-length and on the decoded bytes, so a decompression bomb is refused, and any other content encoding is refused; application/json required; no credentials, and a client id carrying userinfo is refused, because node:https would send it as an Authorization header; a port on fetch's bad-port list (the WHATWG list: 25, 6667, 10080 and the rest) is refused before any connection, and any other port is allowed, as before. The request carries Accept: application/json, Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br and the user-agent fetch sent (node). It is not identical to fetch's: it drops fetch's accept-language: * and sec-fetch-mode: cors, and it asks to close the connection where fetch asked to keep it alive. The address check also refuses the reserved IPv4 blocks it let through (192.0.0.0/24, 192.0.2.0/24, 192.88.99.0/24, 198.18.0.0/15, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24; 240.0.0.0/4 was already refused), and an IPv6 address outside the IPv4 forms AC45 judges is public only in global unicast, 2000::/3, minus 2001::/23 (Teredo, which AC45 left unclassified, benchmarking, ORCHID), 2001:db8::/32, 2002::/16 and 3fff::/20. Pinned clients (Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Codex) never reach this fetch. Usage signal: none new; the existing unknown-client refusal count. Tests: ✅ app/lib/mcp-auth.server.test.ts ("refuses the reserved ranges a public check must not pass", "refuses a client id that carries credentials, which node:https would send", "asks for JSON with a fixed user-agent, sends no credentials, and keeps no TLS session", "refuses a redirect, and every other answer that is not 2xx", "decodes gzip, deflate and br, as fetch did", "refuses a compressed body that decodes past the cap", "refuses a content encoding it does not decode", "refuses the ports fetch refused, and no other", "gives up after one 5-second deadline, whether the headers, the body or its decoding stall", "fetches a public IP-literal host as before", "passes a public answer through the connect-time lookup, in both shapes Node asks for"; on real sockets: "never opens a socket to an IP-literal host that is not public" for https://127.0.0.1/, https://[::1]/ and https://[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]/, "connects only to the answer it checked, so a rebinding resolver gets no second look" (fails on the fetch version: the connection reached the loopback listener), "refuses a name whose answer mixes public and private addresses, before any socket opens", with happy-eyeballs on and off). ❌ Not tested: a real TLS handshake to a public host in CI. Checked by hand on 2026-10-19 from Brad's Mac: a scratch script removed the ChatGPT pin, so https://chatgpt.com/oauth/client.json took the fetch path, and it resolved to ChatGPT through the new path; the host answered brotli-encoded once the request sent Accept-Encoding.
  • AC48 (a refusal says which branch fired — added 2026-10-20, follow-up to AC34): mcp_authorize_refused and mcp_connect_failed may carry a detail, one word from a closed list per reason (MCP_OAUTH_DETAILS in packages/health-core/src/product-events.ts), so the next refusal is diagnosable. Why: 14 refusal rows in 90 days, three of them organic (2026-10-03 no-cookie, 2026-10-07 reviewer-credentials, 2026-10-18 unknown-client from client other), and the row could not say which check fired. The words: unknown-client → malformed (neither our DCR id nor an https URL, or over 4096 characters), dcr-invalid (a DCR id that fails its HMAC or metadata), cimd-refused-url (userinfo, a refused port or a non-public IP literal, before any fetch), cimd-fetch-failed (no usable answer: unreachable, a host that resolves to a private address, a non-2xx status, a non-JSON content type, too large or too slow), cimd-invalid (a body that does not parse, or a client_id that is not the URL fetched), cimd-redirect-refused (redirects we do not allow); redirect-uri → missing, unknown-host, known-host-other-path and loopback-other-path (the same hostname as a registered redirect, differing in anything else; loopback when that registered redirect is a loopback one); resource → other-host, other-path (our host and port, but a different path or scheme; a non-default port is other-host); no-cookie, token-dead-code, token-dead-refresh → missing or unseal-failed (expired and tampered are one word: the seal cannot tell them apart cheaply). A detail is never a URL, host, client id, path, user agent, IP or any free text, and never a health value. The server allow-list keeps a detail only beside its own reason, on those two events; any other word, a detail with no reason, and a detail on any other event are dropped and the row kept. What the client is told does not change: same status, same body, same redirect, whatever the detail. Usage signal: the detail breakdown of the existing two counters. Tests: ✅ app/routes/mcp.hosted.test.ts ("a refusal names its branch in a closed word, and the answer does not change": each word emitted by its branch, every variant of a reason answered identically, reasons without a detail unchanged), app/lib/mcp-auth.server.test.ts ("a refused redirect names how it missed", a wrong scheme on a loopback host included), app/lib/product-events.server.test.ts ("keeps every closed detail word on its own OAuth reason", "drops a detail that is not a closed word, or not its reason's, and keeps the row", "keeps a valid reason and detail when an unrelated key is dropped").

US-33 · I follow the command-line guide and it works — added 2026-09-02

As someone comfortable in a terminal, or an AI coding agent working for me, I can open guides/command-line.md, run the commands in the order written, and get my plan and file a value — without reading the source of US-30 and US-31 to work out what they expect. US-30 and US-31 shipped the two commands; this is the walkthrough that makes them usable by someone who did not build them, and a sample record to practise on so nobody learns them against their own history.

  • AC1 (it works end to end): every command in the guide runs against docs/examples/health-roadmap.sample.json in the order written and exits 0, except the one step the guide documents as a refusal: the occupied-day add exits 1 naming the row that holds the day, and the correction that follows appends a row keeping the original date and flips the old row to entered-in-error.
  • AC2 (the guide cannot drift): tools/walkthrough.test.ts runs that sequence as real subprocesses and asserts the guide's .md still contains each command string it ran, so renaming a flag or a command fails CI instead of leaving a guide that tells the reader to type something that no longer exists.
  • AC3 (the sample is a real record): docs/examples/health-roadmap.sample.json was built through the app's own code paths, not typed by hand, and it loads in the widget's data layer (RoadmapStore.loadLatestMeasurements) with its values current, and through migrateFile unchanged. It is fictional: no part of it came from a person.
  • AC4 (honest first step): the guide states that no command creates a record — the app writes the file when a cloud provider is connected — and says where each backend keeps it, so a reader with no file is not left running commands that refuse.
  • AC5 (2026-09-10, night): get-plan --html writes the report as private as the record it summarises. The file carries the same values, and writeFileSync's mode is filtered by the umask, so on a permissive umask the plan landed world-readable in a shared directory. The write asks for 0600 and a chmodSync follows it, which also tightens a file that already existed. Tests: tools/get-plan.test.ts
  • Usage signal (declared honestly, per the constitution): none from us for the commands themselves, by design — the same reason as US-29/30/31: they run on the user's machine against their own file. The guide is a published page, so the ONE thing that is countable is its traffic: page views and time on /blogs/guides/command-line in the existing site analytics, and GitHub traffic on the repo it sends people to. That measures whether anyone reads it, never whether anyone ran a command. If page views stay flat for a quarter, the guide is not the constraint and writing more of them will not help.
  • Tests: ✅ tools/walkthrough.test.ts (3: AC1/AC2 the guide's eight commands run as real subprocesses in the order written, each asserted still present in the guide's .md, with the occupied-day refusal naming the row, the correction's append-and-flip read back off disk, and the .bak siblings pinned at 3; AC3 the sample through a real RoadmapStore and a migrateFile no-op). ❌ Not tested: git clone and npm ci (run by hand on a fresh clone, 2026-09-02, Node 22.19.0); the rendered HTML is built in CI's reach but read by eye.

US-34 · The record on screen keeps up — added 2026-09-02

As someone with the roadmap open in a tab while my AI assistant edits my record — or with the same record open on my laptop and my phone — I see the change appear where I am looking, instead of wondering whether it worked and reloading the page to find out. US-32 made an assistant able to write; this is the half that makes a write visible to the person it was made for.

  • AC1 (when it re-reads): RoadmapStore.refreshFromRemote() re-reads the record by the two steps of the ordinary SyncManager.load(), the adapter's read and the record's migrate, and merges what comes back with mergeFiles — no second read path, no second source of truth. A missing file is nothing to take in (AC6). It runs when the provider says the file moved, when the tab becomes visible, and when the window takes focus. The provider's own change signal replaced the 60-second timer on 2026-09-02: StorageAdapter.watch(fileName, onChange, signal) is optional, and an adapter that has one never runs the poll. Dropbox holds a files/list_folder/longpoll open against the app folder root (the notify host, which takes no access token — the cursor is the credential; files/list_folder/continue advances it before the store is told), so a write from another device or an assistant arrives in about a second, and a quiet tab costs two requests a minute. Google Drive has no browser long-poll — its push channels need a public webhook — so it walks changes.list from a changes/startPageToken every 3 seconds and calls only when a change names our file id: 20 requests a minute while the tab is visible, and none when it is not. Both back off on failure, doubling to a 60-second ceiling, and re-establish their cursor from scratch. A backend with no watch (GitHub and WebDAV have no cheap one) keeps the 60-second poll. localStorage's watch is the browser's storage event (AC6). A hidden tab watches and polls nothing — it has no screen to keep up to date, and a phone left on a background tab would spend the day holding a connection open; the watch is aborted when the tab is hidden and taken up again on return. A leading-edge 5-second throttle stops focus and visibilitychange — which fire together on a tab switch — making two round trips out of one return, and a push it swallows is held and re-read when the window is out: a watch fires once per change and then goes quiet, so dropping one would lose it. A return's own catch-up is held the same way, never dropped, and a hidden tab runs no re-read, a held one included (AC6).
  • AC2 (a pending local edit always wins): it re-reads NOTHING while a save is in flight or the persist debounce is still pending, and it throws away a merge whose base moved while the read was in the air — the check after the read is that the working copy is the same OBJECT it merged from, because a save can start and finish inside the read window and leave writePending false again by the time the answer lands. The working copy is then AHEAD of the cloud, and merging a read taken before the edit existed would fight the write that is about to go up. The same rule holds on localStorage (AC6).
  • AC3 (only a real change is announced): the merged file is compared to the working copy by CONTENT, with meta excluded — a merge always bumps the file's own clock, and Drive returns no version to compare, so bytes are the only honest test. Unchanged means no event, no re-render and no counted event. Tightened 2026-09-24: the ANNOUNCEMENT, from a re-read or from the change a save folds in, compares what a person would see: rows as a set and no record's own clock (updatedAt, lamport, and since US-10 AC6 fieldStamps). A merge re-sorts rows by id, and on an empty backend the first save trades the page's screenings stamp for the migration's; each was announced as a change, and the page reloaded over a weight being typed (2026-09-22, a guest on localStorage). Taking a merge IN still compares clocks: a skipped clock-only lead would leave the profile lamport behind the cloud's, and the next profile edit would lose the merge.
  • AC4 (how the page hears): the store dispatches a DOM event, hr:remote-changed (REMOTE_CHANGED_EVENT, the same convention as hr:sync-pending-changed), and HealthTool re-runs the load path it already uses after an upload — loadLatestMeasurements, which carries the profile prefill. The store cannot call the API layer itself: the v2 builds alias lib/api to lib/roadmap-data, which imports the store, and the cycle would be real. The listener is registered once, in initRoadmapStore, which is where both surfaces start their data layer. It does nothing while the demographics form is dirty (hasUnsavedProfileEdits, over PREFILL_FIELDS): re-running the load path replaces the form's inputs, and a change landing on a half-entered height would take those keystrokes with it. Nothing is lost, and nothing waits on the user coming back: the change is HELD, and the save that carries the edit up replays it (createRemoteChangeRelay, widget-src/src/lib/remote-replay.ts) — several changes held during one edit collapse into a single re-render. The field the user is typing in rides through the re-render, and a field left with its save still waiting is saved first (2026-09-24): the load path replaces the demographics, never a weight half-typed. Nothing else in the form rides through. A first-time field's value gets none of a matrix draft's checks: it names the row it replaces only as it saves, not as it is typed (still open), and nothing stops it standing in once another writer fills its slot. Carried through a re-read, it would outrank that writer's value in the plan, then correct it. The field being typed in takes that risk, since losing keystrokes is worse; the journey redesign moves these fields onto the draft model. The matrices' drafts are not in the form (2026-09-25): what they lend the plan and the chat lives in its own state, so it rides through every re-read and is judged again against the record just read (US-03 AC6).
  • AC5 (a bug this uncovered, fixed here): a profile-only edit in the app — changing sex, height or birth date with no measurement alongside it — called applyProfileChanges and never called touch(), so it scheduled no save at all and sat in memory until some later unrelated edit carried it up. Every other mutation on the store touches. Fixed in the same commit.
  • AC6 (added 2026-09-25): another tab of the same browser is another writer. A guest's tabs share one on-device record, and a tab took in another tab's save only at its own next save (US-10 AC5). LocalStorageAdapter.watch now listens for the browser's storage event, which fires in every other tab of the origin when one tab writes a key. It calls for the record's key, and for a clear(), which names no key; the version key, other files and the drafts cost nothing. refreshFromRemote drops its local opt-out and keeps AC2's rule, so the re-read, merge, take-in (adopt()) and announcement are the cloud's own. Being watchable, the local tier runs no poll timer. A hidden tab drops any re-read the throttle was holding, and re-reads when shown; that catch-up waits out the throttle rather than being dropped, and the focus and visibilitychange that fire together still cost one read. The local tier's listener holds no connection, so it stays on while the tab is hidden (and from the start, for a tab opened hidden), and a save heard then reads nothing. The return (visibilitychange or focus) re-reads only when the stored revision, the record's version key, differs from the last one this tab took in (one getItem). The store holds that revision, and moves it only for what it merged in: its load, a re-read, and its own writes. A save's verify-after-write read never moves it, since it can see another tab's newer write that the save did not take in (Codex R1 on d19f4d8). A revision is a count plus a random suffix, so a record removed by a log-off and made again never repeats one a hidden tab has seen (Codex R2); only equality is asked of it, so an older bundle's plain count still checks. Residual, while tabs of mixed versions are open after a deploy: a bundle from before 94627c0 computes its next revision as Number("4-abc") + 1, which is NaN, so it writes "1" over any new revision, and a new tab hidden across two such writes can find "1" equal to "1" on return and show a stale record. Display only: every save still reads, merges and checks the version. It ends when the old tabs reload. Until the adversarial review of 2026-09-26 it re-read only if a storage event had been heard while hidden, and a page restored from the back-forward cache or an iOS tab the system suspended can miss that event, so it showed a stale record until its next write. So a lone guest tab never re-reads; until the 2026-09-25 cleanup it re-read and merged the whole record on every return and focus, and found nothing. Cloud tiers still drop the watch while hidden and re-read on every return. Before the Codex review's second round, a held re-read ran after the tab hid, moved the throttle on, and the return's catch-up was dropped, so a save made while the tab was hidden stayed unseen; that held on every backend. A burst of saves in the other tab, a lab import say, costs at most one re-read every 5 seconds, not one per save: the throttle reads the first at once and holds the rest for a trailing re-read. Another tab's erase comes in by the same take-in, so it clears this tab's drafts (US-11 AC6). A re-read never writes, and a missing file, on any backend, is nothing to take in: the empty record migrate makes for one holds no field, and an object with none never wins the merge (US-10 AC6), so the re-read is SyncManager.load() again and the merge changes nothing. Before that rule its fresh stamps beat this tab's profile and screenings wherever their lamport was 0 or absent (a record written by hand or by an older app; found by the Codex review of this AC), and the re-read had to tell a missing file apart itself. So a record another tab removed (a log-off, or a cloud erase wiping the device copy) brings nothing in: this tab keeps what it shows and any edit it has not saved, and puts nothing back. Following the removal instead would suit a log-off, but it would destroy rows this tab saved since the other tab last lifted the record, which may exist nowhere else; a file made again can be erased again, a dropped copy is gone. Its next save does make the device file again from its own copy (US-10 AC5's residual). That save merges the missing file as the empty record, which since US-10 AC6's empty-object rule leaves a profile or screenings with no lamport as it was; before, it emptied them. Residuals: the event's propagation, the throttle and a pending edit here each delay a take-in. The usage signal below counts these take-ins too: HealthTool fires remote_change_applied for every announced change, whatever wrote it. So since this AC a count no longer shows by itself that an assistant or a second device is at work; a guest's second tab counts as well, and since 2026-09-26 backend: local tells it apart. A cloud count still does not tell another cloud tab, a second device or an assistant apart. And one burst of saves in the other tab, a lab import say, can count twice: the throttle's leading re-read and its trailing one each announce.
  • Usage signal (declared, per the constitution): remote_change_applied in product_events — fired by HealthTool when it has actually re-rendered on a remote change. Its one metadata key, since 2026-09-26, is backend: local (another guest tab of this browser) or cloud (the record lives in a cloud; the change came from another tab, another device or an assistant), a closed list the server's schema enforces. Only guest tabs split out: cloud does not tell another cloud tab from another device or an assistant. Never which field changed, never a value. Read against results_viewed: if it stays at zero once the connector guides are out, either nobody is running an assistant against a record they also have open, or the re-read is not firing — and the two are told apart by whether hosted MCP tool calls are happening at all.

US-35 · My assistant imports my lab files — built 2026-09-04, verified live 2026-09-05 (hosted API on the scratch Dropbox: commit, replay, conflicts, 90-day rule, documents; ChatGPT drag + folder routes on Brad's record, extract only; Drive refusal)

As someone who keeps a ZIP of lab PDFs and clinic letters (Brad's own is health.zip), I can drop the file into my connected Dropbox folder and say "import it", or drag it into ChatGPT and say the same, and my assistant reads every document, shows me what it found against what my record already holds, and files only what I confirm — instead of retyping thirty numbers or leaving the chat for the website. The website's upload already does extraction, review and a bulk save (lab-upload.md); this is the same pipeline reached through the connector, with the review step done in words. Design brief and the resolved decisions from its adversarial review: mcp-import-design.md. Architecture context: mcp-architecture.md §3, §7.

  • AC1 (one tool, two phases, and the first never writes): a single tool import_documents in packages/health-core/src/mcp-tools.ts, published on every surface like the other seven. Called with a source (AC2, AC4) it EXTRACTS and returns candidates plus a receipt; called with commit (AC8) it WRITES; commit beside a source is refused. An extract call opens the record read-only and saves nothing, ever — a test asserts the record's version is unchanged after an extract that found values. The server keeps nothing between the two phases: the candidate payload is parked in the USER's own folder (AC7).
  • AC2 (the folder route, Dropbox): with no file argument the tool lists the ROOT of the connected app folder (dropboxListFolder, files only, has_more followed) and takes the files named in fileNames, or every importable file when the argument is absent. Importable is .pdf, .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .zip by the shared isImportableEntryName rule; health-roadmap.json, folders, dotfiles and everything else are ignored, not refused. A name in fileNames is matched by equality against the listing and the file is downloaded by the listing's id, so a name never forms a path; a name not in the listing refuses the call and names what the folder holds. Five files per call by default (IMPORT_FILES_PER_CALL), the rest come back in remaining with next telling the assistant to commit this receipt first, then call again with those names; a file not reached inside the budget (AC10) comes back skipped: "time" AND in remaining — on the drag route too, where next asks for the ZIP again after the commit (2026-09-07). A folder that holds no PDF, JPEG, PNG or ZIP refuses in words naming the folder and the four types.
  • AC3 (Google Drive, honestly): the folder route on a Drive connection is refused in words, not attempted: the connector holds drive.file, which sees only files this app created or the user opened through Google's picker — a file the user drops into the folder is invisible to it (Google's scope definition, confirmed 2026-09-04; GOOGLE_DRIVE_SCOPE in drive-rest.ts). The refusal is per client and puts the way that works for THAT assistant first: ChatGPT → drag the file into the chat from a desktop browser, or the website's upload; Claude and everything else → the website's upload. Dragging into ChatGPT works on a Drive connection because the bytes come from ChatGPT, not the folder. Counted as mcp_import {route: drive_refused}. Widening the scope is not on the table: drive.readonly is a restricted scope with a security assessment attached, for a feature whose alternative is a drag.
  • AC4 (the ChatGPT file route — deleted 2026-09-10 on Brad's decision, 27 days early): the tool descriptor carried _meta["openai/fileParams"]: ["file"] and an input field file whose schema declared exactly download_url, file_id (required) and mime_type, file_name (optional) — the shape OpenAI's reference required — and the server fetched download_url and nothing else: https only, host on an exact allow-list (files.oaiusercontent.com, plus anything in CHATGPT_FILE_HOSTS; the region-suffixed Azure blob family ^oaisdmntprn[a-z0-9]*\.blob\.core\.windows\.net$ was dropped 2026-09-10 because it was a namespace, not a list — any Azure account named oaisdmntprn… passed it), a refused host warned by hostname only, redirect: "error", a 10-second abort, a 20 MB byte cap through readCappedBytes, and the type decided by magic bytes (%PDF-, PK\x03\x04, JPEG, PNG), never by the declared mime_type or the file name. A bare chat_upload://… reference — what the phone apps hand over — was a schema error whose message was the mobile sentence. All of it is now deleted: the argument, the fetch, the host list, IMPORT_REFUSALS.mobile/dragFallback and the chatgpt_file/chatgpt_refused counters. What is left is one guard line in runImport: a call still carrying file — a tool list cached before 2026-09-07 — is answered with IMPORT_REFUSALS.refresh, and nothing is fetched. Claude cannot pass a file to a remote tool at all; the tool description says the folder route is the Claude way.
  • AC5 (one extraction pipeline, not a second): every file goes through the existing extractOrClassify (app/lib/anthropic.server.ts, UNIFIED_SYSTEM_PROMPT, unit resolution) — the same call the website makes — with httpAttempts: 1 (no HTTP retry on this path; since 2026-10-16 no path has an outer retry, US-15 AC34) and a timeout of min(20 s, what is left of the budget), so one model call ends inside the deadline by construction — and the second call, made when the first answer does not parse (the same request re-sent; it was a { prefill until 2026-10-16, US-15 AC34), shares that same deadline (extractOrClassify computes one until for both calls; it gets what is left, never a fresh window; tested with a spy on AbortSignal.timeout). Non-lab documents are asked for metadata only (documentMode: 'metadata': title, date, a one-line summary ≤120 chars, contentMarkdown empty, 3072 tokens since 2026-10-16, 2048 before, US-15 AC34), since the connector files no text; the website's upload keeps the full-transcription prompt (unifiedSystemPrompt('full'), the same head and response format). Every other I/O in the call is ABORTED at the same deadline, not abandoned (2026-09-04): runImport starts one clock per call — 40 s, ImportSurface.budgetMs — before it reads the record, and every adapter call the call makes carries a deadlineSignal derived from it: the record's read and write through SyncManager (load/save take a signal and pass it to read/write/verify), the folder listing, each download, the stale-pending sweep, the ChatGPT file fetch, the pending-file write in stash, and the commit's read and delete of the pending file. StorageAdapter's read/write/readDocument/list/remove take that signal as an optional last argument; the Dropbox and Drive REST adapters hand it to fetch (fetchOrFail joins it with the adapter's own 30 s bound via AbortSignal.any), so a provider that took the socket and went quiet is cut off at the deadline and its promise rejects with a TimeoutError; the memory and file adapters refuse to start once it is aborted. What the assistant sees: a hung listing or pending-file read is a refusal, a hung download is skipped: "time", a hung pending write refuses the extract, a hung delete is swallowed and swept later, and a hung record read or write surfaces as the provider's "did not answer" refusal. An extract's downloads and model calls end 4 s before the deadline (BUDGET_RESERVE_MS), leaving that reserve for slotting and the stash. Nothing an import does runs past the deadline. A PDF is passed to the model whole, as a base64 document content block (the 'pdf' page type in lab-extraction.ts's pagesToContentBlocks, verified with one real Haiku call 2026-09-04: 3,369 input tokens for a one-page PDF; the website's text|image route schema untouched). Images go as image blocks; a ZIP is opened server-side with JSZip (already in the Fly image, now declared in the root manifest) under caps: 20 MB per ZIP, 20 importable entries, 5 MB per entry INFLATED — the central directory's declared size is only the cheap first refusal, the bytes are counted as they inflate and the stream is stopped past the cap. Entries are taken by position, typed by magic bytes, and nested zips are skipped by name. Each entry is named <zip>/<path inside it> (labs.zip/Blood tests/lipids.pdf), as the website's upload names it since 2026-10-13 (US-12 AC9): control-stripped, and cut once, by zipMemberName from the whole raw path (unzip never cuts a name), at 255 characters, keeping the member's own end plus ~ and a hash of the whole name, it is the name in files, the file a fileDates answer gives back, the hint naming a twin, and the document's sourceFileName. So two ZIPs holding one path are two files in one call, and one member has one sourceFileName on both surfaces, which the name rule for hashless rows needs (AC6). fileNames and remaining still name the ZIP itself, the file in the folder root. Before 2026-10-13 the connector named an entry by its path alone. Those rows carry a contentHash, so reading the same ZIP again is still already_imported; a hashless website row named by the path alone (uploaded before 2026-10-13 with no original archived: off-cloud, or a failed blob write) no longer matches by name, so that member is offered again. The junk filter (__MACOSX/, .DS_Store, dotfiles at any depth, Thumbs.db) lives in health-core and the widget's zip-extract.ts calls it. Since 2026-10-18 that pipeline also reads a DATED previous-results column for the website (US-12 AC12). The connector skips previous columns for now: prepareImport leaves out any value carrying its own day on the folder route, uncounted and with no new hint: its tool text and its no-previous-column rule are unchanged, while its extraction quality changed (below). Held until OpenAI's review of MCP 1.0.2 ends (coordinator, 2026-10-18); until then dated previous columns are website-only, and the connector's metadata prompt keeps the base rule (every previous column ignored), with the prepareImport guard as the backstop. Recorded plainly: the connector's extraction rules DID change under the review (2026-10-18), while its tool text and its no-previous-column behaviour did not. The shared prompt now copies units as printed and never guesses one (an empty unit when none is printed, US-21 AC7), reads printed reference ranges, and suggests the catalogue's keys (US-21 AC4); a model's own question keeps the inferred-unit note beside it (US-21 AC18); and an inferred unit that fits both scales is flagged low (US-21 AC18). A lab row printed with no unit is still refused on this route, as before (appendLabValue, the dry run behind add_lab_values, file_results and import_documents, keeps requiring a unit while the assistant tools are under review). The assistant route (file_results) keeps its own per-line recordedAt (US-36 AC1). Test: mcp-tools.test.ts "AC5/AC13 — import_documents does not offer a previous-column value".
  • AC6 (what the record already holds): every extracted value is slotted against the record by the one rule the website's review table uses — findActiveInSlot + slotState in record-edits.ts, core-metric equality on the DISPLAYED string so float noise never manufactures a conflict (for core metrics the website's table compares the stored canonical value instead since 2026-10-13, US-13 AC3; the connector still compares the displayed string, so it reads two values one display step apart as held_equal: Lp(a) 124 and 125 nmol/L in a US-units record until mg/dL took one decimal place (2026-10-13; now "49.6" and "50.0"), and still 124.5 and 125 nmol/L, both "125", in an SI record: open): free, held_equal (already recorded; accepting it writes nothing), or held_different with the existing row id and value, and replaceable when the held row is inside the hosted 90-day correction window. Candidates are shown in the record's own unit system (profile.unitSystem, default SI: displayValue/displayUnit for a US user read "131 mg/dL", not "3.4 mmol/L"), stored canonical, and core-metric slot equality is judged in that system (2026-09-07). Additional-lab equality is sameLabQuantity in record-edits.ts, shared by the website's review table and the connector (Brad 2026-10-16; PR #145 from Austin Bell plus the website half): the record holds a catalogued lab in SI, a report prints its own unit, so each side is converted to the catalogue's SI unit under its own name (BUN keeps its factor), float noise is ignored, and a unit the catalogue refuses is never equal; an uncatalogued test compares reported value and unit, spelling folded ("umol/L" is "µmol/L") but case kept ("G/L", a cell count, is not "g/L", a mass). The website keys a lab row by the connector's labSlotKey, so a report's "Vitamin D" and the stored vitamin_d share one row, and a cell whose unit is not its row's shows its own unit; a ticked Replace is skipped only when it is the same quantity. Before 2026-10-16 both compared bare numbers: 50 ng/mL offered over a held 50 nmol/L read as already recorded, and on the website the two sat in separate rows, so the collision was never seen. Preview numbers and units stay as reported. Two files offering one (metric, day) in one call are BOTH offered, the second marked sameDayAs the first, so a preliminary and a final report are seen, not silently dropped. A document is already_imported hash-first: when a live documents[] row carries its bytes' contentHash (sha256-<hex>, the same field the website's archive keys on — ONE dedup key for both writers), or by sourceFileName ONLY against a live row that has no hash (a pre-hash website row) — a lab portal that names every download Results.pdf must not make the second report "already imported" (2026-09-07; before, the name alone blocked it with no way past). The same bytes under two names in ONE call (a browser's Results.pdf + Results (1).pdf) file one row: the twin is already_imported with a hint naming the first file ("The same file as Results.pdf in this call"), so two rows never share the archive key (2026-09-07; before, both landed, the website's upload could tombstone only one and re-offered the other on every upload). It is not sent to the model again, and the entry's hint names the row's file and date ("the same file was filed on … as …" / "a file with this name was filed on … and that row carries no fingerprint… Rename the file to import it"). A ChatGPT drag with no file_name is named from its bytes (file-<sha8>.pdf), never a shared word that would dedup every later nameless drag. The website's bulkSaveDocuments treats a hash on a row WITH a fileRef as "already archived" and a hash on a row WITHOUT one as the connector's metadata-only import: uploading that same PDF on the website writes the blob into a new row and tombstones the metadata-only one — only once the blob write succeeds; a failed write leaves the connector row live so its hash still dedups — so the original gets archived rather than silently skipped. A value the record would refuse — out of range, a future day, a core metric under a lab name — is dropped at extract time with the reason, by a dry run of the same appendMeasurement/appendLabValue the write tools use, so the receipt never carries a value the record would not take. A lab report with no usable collection date is failed: no_date with the ask-the-user hint; the caller's fileDates: {name: 'YYYY-MM-DD'} on the next call supplies it (AC13).
  • AC7 (the receipt): the extract writes its payload — candidates plus document metadata, never document text — to the user's folder as imports/pending-<uuid>.json through the same adapter that holds the record, and the receipt the assistant carries is that file's own id, a plain lowercase UUID (36 characters; MAX_RECEIPT_LENGTH is 64). The file is {v: 2, payload, issued, mac}: issued in epoch seconds, and mac 32 lowercase hex characters (128 bits) of HMAC-SHA256 under an HKDF key from MCP_SEAL_KEYS with info mcp/import-step/v1, distinct from every blob type's. The MAC covers the kind, the id, issued, the payload's sha256, the connection hash, and the client and resource hashes. It is signed with the first key and checked against every configured key, so a rotation inside the hour does not strand a receipt; a key since removed opens nothing. Commit checks, in this order and BEFORE anything is charged, so a forged or foreign receipt costs nothing and deletes nothing: the UUID shape (else not valid); the pending file (missing: "That receipt names no pending import: it was committed, discarded or mistyped. Nothing was written. Extract again if the user still wants it."); its shape, v 2 (else not readable); the MAC for this connection and client, compared with timingSafeEqual (else not valid for this connection); the one-hour window, with an issued up to 60 s ahead of our clock taken as skew and more refused as not valid (else expired). Then the candidate ids, then the charge, then the write, then the delete; a second commit of the same receipt finds nothing and refuses. Changed 2026-10-07: the receipt was a ~550-byte sealed 'import' blob. Nothing in it was secret, and in the 1.0.2 demo run ChatGPT's approval card called it an "opaque or disguised payload" and once blocked the commit. A pending file from before the change has no v, refuses as not readable, and is swept by name; a sealed blob sent now is over the schema's 64 characters and gets the malformed-commit refusal. A commit deletes the file it consumed at once, best effort: a delete that fails is one Sentry count carrying no file name, no path and no error text, and what it costs is a file that outlives its use, not a leak of anything the user did not already own. There is no discard action — an import the user declines is simply never committed, and its file is swept. The sweep is the backstop, not the cleanup: it takes imports/pending-*.json files older than twice a receipt's life (two hours, past which nothing can still be committed from one), never another file the user keeps in that folder. Two changes on 2026-09-10, from the adversarial review: the window was 24 h, and the sweep ran only inside extract — which file_results and every Google Drive user never call, so their abandoned pending files were never swept at all. It now runs in stash, the one door every route passes through, so the next import of any kind clears the last one's residue. The assistant can only SELECT candidate ids (accept, replace); it cannot edit a value or invent a document, which is why this write may land documents[] rows when add_lab_values may not (US-32 AC5). A payload the model retyped is exactly add_lab_values, which exists. Changed 2026-10-07 (later): a commit also carries approval, the user’s own words approving these candidates, quoted from their message (1 to 200 characters). ChatGPT's safety layer blocked a correct_value confirm whose call carried "a confirmation receipt but no evidence of the user's own-word approval" (its approval card, the same day), and a commit is the same kind of call. On the hosted server the check comes first in open, before the pending file is read, the ids are checked or anything is charged: a missing or blank approval is refused with "If the user has not yet answered in their own words, show them the candidates and end your turn. Otherwise commit again with the same receipt and approval set to the user’s own words approving these candidates, quoted from their message. Nothing was written.", and the pending file stays for the honest commit. One over 200 characters fails the schema and gets the malformed-commit refusal, which now names approval. The call has already loaded the record by then (runImport reads it before any commit opens); nothing else is touched. Privacy: the words live in memory for one request and are never stored, logged, hashed, counted or echoed back. The stdio server accepts the field and ignores it. Tests: app/lib/mcp-import.server.test.ts (including the words never reaching the record or the pending file), tools/mcp-server.test.ts.
  • AC8 (the commit): all-or-nothing. Accepted free candidates and replaced held_different ones land through bulkAppendValues — the same pure function the website's bulkSaveMeasurements/bulkSaveLabValues now call — core metrics as measurements in SI, the rest as lab values in the lab's own unit (superseded 2026-09-18: a catalogued lab test is stored in its SI unit, US-21 phase 3; an uncatalogued one still keeps the unit it was reported in), with source: "lab_import"; a replace supersedes the held row with correctsId and flips it to entered-in-error, after the commit's own two checks — the held row still carries the id and value the receipt names (the expectedValue guard), and replaceable computed at extract against the surface's 90-day rule (enforced ONCE, here; the receipt's hash keeps it honest); a held_different id in accept but not replace writes nothing — silence is not consent. Each extracted file, lab report included, lands as a documents[] row metadata-only unless already_imported (fileRef: "", contentHash: "sha256-<hex>" of the bytes, the sniffed mimeType, extractedText: "", metadata: {importedVia: "connector"}), and the original stays where the user put it until the website archives it (AC6). A lab report's row is the shape the website's upload writes for the same PDF (synthesizeLabArchiveEntries: pathology_report, title "Blood test results", the report date), which the website's Documents list hides — the values are the record, the row is the file. A row records the file, not acceptance: a commit that declines every value still files it (live 2026-09-05, defect A: lab reports got no row, so a re-extract re-read and re-charged the file and the website had no row to archive the blob behind). The commit re-reads the record fresh: a slot whose active row moved since the extract (a different id or value, or a free slot now taken) refuses the WHOLE commit, naming the slot, and the assistant extracts again. Two chosen candidates for one (metric, day) — sameDayAs — refuse the whole commit in words ("c2 and c1 both name ldl on …; the record keeps one value per metric per day. Pick one."), never a contract error. A document needs no selection: a clinic letter yields zero candidates, so the only commit it can get is an empty one, and that commit files the letter (already_imported keeps it from landing twice). So the extract must not read as "nothing to do" (live 2026-09-05 it did — "0 value(s) are new" — and ChatGPT never offered to file the letter): the extract result carries documents (source name, title bounded per AC9, type, date), its next says how many documents can be filed and that a commit with empty accept and replace files them, and the tool description says the same; titles stay out of next, the field the assistant follows. A commit whose accept and replace are both empty AND whose payload holds no unfiled document writes nothing, changes no version, and says so. For live testing against a real record: the first empty commit of a lab report files one metadata-only row and nothing else; the same file extracted again is already_imported and carries no receipt. Not atomic across devices: a second device writing the same slot at the same moment leaves two actives until the next merge demotes the newer one, as with every write; the commit's text says so.
  • AC9 (nothing kept, and who sees what): bytes are held in memory for one request and dropped; no file, no value and no extracted text is written anywhere on our side; the tool result and the pending payload carry numbers, units, dates, file names, a classification and title/summary/question bounded to 120 printable characters and labelled as text from the document — never contentMarkdown, extractedText or the extractor's free-form metadata; next, the field the assistant follows, carries counts and ids only, never any of the three. UNIFIED_SYSTEM_PROMPT tells the model the document is data, not instructions; a document whose only content is an instruction block reaches the assistant as a bounded title and no candidates. The mcp_tool_call counter stays {tool, client, outcome}; Sentry gets a fixed message ("import_documents: extraction failed"), the error class and the file kind only — never the thrown error itself, whose parse message quotes the model's output (tested with a fake Sentry, 2026-09-07); no log line carries a file name or a value (tested). What DOES change, and is disclosed rather than hidden: on this route the file is sent to Anthropic's API under OUR key for extraction — the tool's own description says it at the step it happens ("each file's contents go to Anthropic for extraction at this step, kept by neither of us", 2026-09-10), and the consent screen, the privacy addendum, the ChatGPT listing's Compliance section, both connector guides, agent-access.md, lab-upload.md, the architecture map and the READMEs say so, and say that the website's upload instead keeps the PDF in the browser.
  • AC10 (bounds): an extract spends 1 + 1 per file of the connection's 60 weighted writes an hour — the 1 is the tool's declared cost: 'add' charged by the loop's beforeCall like every write, the per-file charge goes through the same chargeWrites before each model call (so a refused file still costs, and there is ONE refusal wording); a commit spends 1 + 5 per replace (charged after the receipt verifies AND every id is checked against the payload, so invented ids cost nothing); 30 files per connection per day (IMPORT_FILES_PER_DAY = IMPORT_LIMITS.filesPerDay, the importFiles counter beside the write allowance in mcp-grants.server.ts, keyed on the connection hash) — a file whose model call timed out is refunded on both file counters, since it was never read (2026-09-07); the website's per-machine daily file cap (AI_DAILY_FILE_CAP) is one createQuotaCounter both callers spend from (machineFiles in rate-limiter.ts). All three counters are per machine, so the real ceiling is × machines × 2 Fly apps. Files are extracted three at a time under a whole-call budget of 40 s (MCP_IMPORT_BUDGET_MS; ChatGPT cuts a tool call at 60 s), and what is not reached is skipped: "time" or remaining, never half-answered. unrecognized is capped at 50 lines a call (MAX_UNRECOGNIZED_LINES), 120 characters each.
  • AC11 (the local server): the stdio server holds no model key and opens no socket (US-32 AC7), so import_documents there refuses in one sentence pointing at the website or the hosted connector. It stays in the list: one tool list on every surface, no hosted-only subset to drift. A local-path variant was not built: the local server has no model to read a file with.
  • AC12 (every place a tool is named moves together): MCP_TOOL_NAMES (parity test), OUTPUTS, the prompts list (a fourth prompt, "Import my lab files"), the guards test's hand-written name list, the consent page's capability list, the privacy addendum, chatgpt-app-listing.md (annotations table, three justifications, a starter prompt, two test cases, the Compliance sentence), agent-access.md, mcp-architecture.md §3, both connector guides, getting-started.md, reference.md's inventory, deploy-runbook-mcp.md's verify sequence, the architecture map, both READMEs, .env.example. Annotations, honestly: not read-only, destructive (a replace flips a row for good), not idempotent, open-world (it reaches Anthropic's API; it stopped reaching OpenAI's file host when the drag route was deleted, 2026-09-10).
  • AC13 (when it cannot, the user hears why and what to do — 2026-09-07, from the heavy review and a live ChatGPT drag trial): one closed table, packages/health-core/src/import-hints.ts, maps every file reason to a sentence naming the limit and the way round it — unsupported (the accepted types "PDF, JPEG, PNG or ZIP"; HEIC: share as JPEG or take a screenshot, since ChatGPT's composer drops HEIC silently), too_large (5 MB per PDF or image, 20 MB per ZIP; the website's upload takes 10 MB), no_date (ask the user the date, call again with fileDates), bad_date (2026-09-07, live trial: a fileDates day the record refuses — future, or not a calendar day — is said back in the record's own words, "2030-01-01 has not happened yet", and asks for the correct date; before, it fell through to no_date and the assistant asked for the date the user had just given), quota (30 files a day per connection, resets a day after the first), allowance, time (ask again after the commit; filed files cost nothing), unreadable, too_many, and (2026-10-19, Brad) the two extraction stops (US-15 AC34), which until then fell under unreadable and its "a clearer scan usually works", advice that is wrong for both and sent assistants back to retry the same file: too_long (the model hit max_tokens: "This file is too long to read in one go. Upload it on drstanfield.com/pages/roadmap, which reads longer reports, or split it into smaller files and import those." The website is named first because the connector reads at 3,072 output tokens and the website at 10,000) and refused (the model declined: "This file could not be read, and trying again will not help. Ask the user for the values, or to enter them on drstanfield.com/pages/roadmap."). One sentence could not be true for both, so each has its own; neither names a classifier or a policy. The two codes are not yet in the reason field's published list, because the tool text is frozen during the 1.0.2 review (app/lib/mcp-freeze.test.ts pins the hashes of INSTRUCTIONS, MCP_TOOLS, MCP_PROMPTS and SERVER_INFO at cab5615a); the hint carries the meaning. After the verdict the two codes join the published list — and the whole-call refusals: empty folder ("no PDF, JPEG, PNG or ZIP files in the folder root (Apps/Health Plan by Dr Brad)"), malformed commit or arguments; a Dropbox 401/403 on a download is rethrown as its StorageError so the route answers with the existing reconnect hint instead of unreadable. Every files[] entry that was not read carries hint; next is short — the counts, one instruction, the continuation (commit this receipt first, then…) — and names where detail lives (hint, question ids, unrecognized count, sameDayAs) (the drag route's extra fallback line went with the route on 2026-09-10). The tool description leads with a fixed sentence ChatGPT's consent card can reuse (since 2026-09-10: "Reads lab files … the user put in their Dropbox folder … and writes nothing to your record until you confirm; the candidates wait in a pending file in your own folder, deleted when you confirm; one nobody confirms expires in an hour with its receipt and is swept two hours on, at your next import.") and the two routes as a numbered choice, so a text-only "import my labs" turn offers the folder (live 2026-09-07 it only said "upload the file"); _meta invocation text is "Importing your documents…" / "Import step done" — one string covers both phases, and the keys match the Apps SDK reference as of 2026-09-07. The limits the sentences name are defined once (IMPORT_LIMITS) and the server's caps derive from them. With previous columns skipped on this route (AC5, 2026-10-18), a fileDates answer moves the primary column's values and nothing else; the argument's text is unchanged during the 1.0.2 review.
  • AC14 (2026-09-10): the lab-import poll is addressed by a token the caller holds, not by a guessable id, so one uploader cannot read another's pending extract. Tests: app/routes/api.lab-import-v2.test.ts, widget-src/src/lib/upload-api.test.ts
  • AC15 (2026-09-10, late): the poll is a POST and its token rides in the body. Nothing secret and nothing about a person's health now travels in a logged URL on this route. Tests: app/routes/api.lab-import-v2.test.ts, widget-src/src/lib/upload-api.test.ts
  • AC16 (PLANNED, not built; Brad 2026-10-19: after OpenAI's verdict on MCP 1.0.2): import_documents reads a Word .docx the way the website does (US-12 AC13). Today a .docx in the folder sniffs as a ZIP, holds nothing importable, and is skipped. The build: tell a .docx from a ZIP by its word/document.xml part; move the browser's docx-extract.ts reader into health-core so both surfaces share it (the shared inflateCapped already lives there); add .docx to the folder's import extensions and accepted types; update the tool description and hints in the same change, which is why it waits for the verdict. Needs the full adversary + Codex review (agent contract).
  • AC17 (2026-10-19, PR #163): The shared bulk writer validates each core measurement's metric name, finite numeric value and existing plausibility bounds before touching its slot or correction target. Typed measurementRefusals identify invalid core rows separately from duplicates and lab-unit refusals; an invalid correction cannot supersede a valid row or claim the slot against a later valid input. A refusal's message names the reason, never the value, as LabUnitRefusal's does; an out-of-range refusal also carries bound (above or below), which end of the range it missed. The website shows each refusal the way it shows a refused lab unit: a settled outcome, not a save error, so the done screen names the test once on its own line and offers no retry (US-12 AC6). The line says what is out of range: the test's name and the end of the range it missed, in the unit the person reads (Lp(a) in its field's own unit: nmol/L, mg/dL or mg/L), never the value. That end is the SI bound the record enforced, converted and rounded inward, so the value is always past the number shown: LDL's 12.9 mmol/L reads "above 498 mg/dL", since 499 mg/dL is refused; the form's US-unit messages round the same way ("at most 498 mg/dL", "at least 45 lbs") (Brad, 2026-10-20: "explain what's out of range, otherwise it will confuse users"): "PSA not saved: above 10,000 ng/mL, the highest value this tool accepts. Check the report, then enter it again.", or "below 9 mmol/mol, the lowest value…" for a floor. A connector commit containing a refused core row is rejected as a whole before any selected values or documents are written. Lab conversion and receipt semantics are unchanged. One clinical bound moved (Brad, 2026-10-19, raised again 2026-10-20): the PSA ceiling is 10,000 ng/mL, up from 100, because metastatic prostate cancer can read in the hundreds or thousands. It holds on the form and the upload alike. evidence.ts and roadmap_text.html state no PSA maximum, so they do not change. The triglycerides, LDL and Lp(a) ceilings stay. Usage signal: measurement_refused, sent by the browser once per tab for each metric and reason, with metadata { refusal }, one of MEASUREMENT_REFUSAL_REASONS (unknown-metric, invalid-value, out-of-range), plus metric, a METRIC_TYPES id, for invalid-value only (MEASUREMENT_REFUSALS_WITH_METRIC). An unknown-metric name is free text; an out-of-range metric would tell analytics this visitor's value for that test is past a clinical bound (Brad, 2026-10-20), and the server refuses that row. The browser still counts one event per tab for each (metric, refusal) pair: an out-of-range metric keys the tab's throttle locally and is never sent. Never the value. It is not lab_unit_refused, whose rows list spellings to teach the catalogue. Tests: record-edits.test.ts, mcp-tools.test.ts, validation.test.ts (the PSA ceiling of 10,000 ng/mL: 9,999 kept, 10,001 refused; every metric's schema bounds are its unit table's SI range; the PSA message keeps its comma in US units), app/lib/product-events.server.test.ts (the counter's two closed words; no metric beside out-of-range), widget-src/src/lib/local-first-data.test.ts, widget-src/src/lib/product-events.test.ts (one send per metric and refusal; two out-of-range metrics send twice, neither naming its metric), widget-src/src/lib/lab-value-labels.test.ts (one wording per reason; the range's end and unit, SI, US and Lp(a) in mg/L; for LDL 499.5 and 500 mg/dL, HbA1c 20 %, creatinine 0.1 and 30 mg/dL, weight 44 lbs, waist 79 in, Lp(a) 3001 mg/L and PSA 10,001 ng/mL, the stated end is past the typed number and itself accepted; the line and the form's message agree), UploadModal.session.test.tsx (the lines in review, in a live region, cleared on a new Save) and InputPanel.psa-range.test.tsx (the PSA field takes the unit table's range; 9,999 kept and 10,001 cleared on blur), record-edits.test.ts (an uploaded PSA of 9,999 saved, 10,001 refused above the range); synthetic fixtures.
  • AC18 (2026-10-20, Brad): stash parks the pending file FIRST and sweeps stale ones AFTER. The sweep used to run beside the park, and on Dropbox its deletes drew a 429 that refused the park, so the user saw "The candidates could not be parked". A refused park still answers with that refusal, and it is no longer silent: one Sentry warning, mcp_import: candidates not parked, tagged with the error class (a closed list: StorageError, TimeoutError, AbortError, else other) and the HTTP status. Never the error message, which names the file (AC9). A refused park skips that call's sweep (the provider just pushed back; the next stash sweeps). The sweep's own failures stay one count and never fail the call. Not covered: a 429 from another writer in the same account (the user's tab saving, two imports at once) still refuses the park, with no retry; the warning count shows how often. Tests: app/lib/mcp-import.server.test.ts ("US-35 AC18": an adapter that 429s a write while a delete is in flight; the order is write, list, remove; a refused park runs no sweep; the refused park's Sentry call carries only errorClass and httpStatus).
  • Usage signal (declared, per the constitution): mcp_tool_call with tool: "import_documents" covers success and refusal. One more event, value-free: mcp_import with route (dropbox | drive_refused | assistant; the two ChatGPT-drag values went with the route on 2026-09-10), phase (extract | commit) and files as a bucket (0 | 1 | 2-5 | 6-20). It answers the one question that decides the feature's shape — which route people actually use, and whether the Drive refusal is met often enough to be worth a different answer. Never a file name, never a value, never a count precise enough to identify a record. The extraction stops (too_long, refused, AC13, 2026-10-19) add nothing to mcp_import: the published privacy page describes that row as route, phase and a file-count bucket, and it does not change during the 1.0.2 review.
